70273.e: Angles between 180° and 360° are called reflex angles. 250° is in this range.
70273.m: Reflex angles are between 180 and 360 degrees.

70274.q: How many degrees does a full turn have?
70274.e: A full turn is one whole rotation, and one whole rotation has 360°.

70275.q: What type of angle is an angle of 35°?
70275.e: Angles greater than 0° and less than 90° are called acute angles.
70275.m: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle.

70276.q: By how many degrees does the minute hand of a clock turn in 15 minutes?
70276.e: In 60 minutes the minute hand turns 360°. In 15 minutes it is a quarter of that, so 360° ÷ 4 gives 90°.
70276.m: In a quarter of an hour the minute hand turns through a right angle.

70277.q: Two angles lie next to each other on a straight line. One measures 125°. How big is the other?
70277.e: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. So 180° minus 125° gives 55°.
70277.m: Angles on a straight line always add up to 180 degrees.

70278.q: Two straight lines cross, and one angle measures 70°. How big is the vertically opposite angle?
70278.e: Vertically opposite angles lie opposite each other at the crossing point and are always equal.
70278.m: Vertically opposite angles are always equal.

70279.q: What is the sum of the interior angles in every triangle?
70279.e: If you place the three angles of a triangle next to each other, together they make a straight angle of 180°.
70279.m: In every triangle the three angles add up to 180 degrees.

70280.q: In a right-angled triangle, one acute angle measures 34°. How big is the other acute angle?
70280.e: The angle sum is 180°, and the right angle is 90°. So 180° minus 90° minus 34° gives 56°.
70280.m: The two acute angles of a right-angled triangle add up to 90 degrees.

70281.q: In an isosceles triangle, the angle at the top measures 40°. How big is each base angle?
70281.e: The base angles are equal. (180° minus 40°) ÷ 2 gives 70°.
70281.m: In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal.

70282.q: The base angles of an isosceles triangle each measure 52°. How big is the angle at the top?
70282.e: The two base angles add up to 104°. That leaves 180° minus 104°, which gives 76°.
70282.m: You find the third angle by subtracting the known angles from 180 degrees.

70283.q: Can a triangle have two right angles?
70283.e: Two right angles already make 180°. There would be nothing left for the third angle, so it is impossible.
70283.m: A triangle has at most one right angle.

70284.q: What is the sum of the interior angles in a pentagon?
70284.e: A pentagon can be split into 3 triangles from one corner. 3 times 180° gives 540°.
70284.m: You get the angle sum of a polygon by splitting it into triangles.

70285.q: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. How big is the largest angle?
70285.e: There are 6 equal parts making 180° together, so one part is 30°. The largest angle has 3 parts, so 90°.
70285.m: With angles in a ratio, you first divide 180 degrees by the sum of the parts.

70286.q: A triangle has the interior angles 50° and 60°. How big is the exterior angle at the third corner?
70286.e: The third interior angle measures 70°, so its exterior angle is 180° minus 70°, which gives 110°. That is exactly the sum of the other two interior angles.
70286.m: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the two opposite interior angles added together.

70287.q: What is a triangle with three sides of equal length called?
70287.e: If all three sides are the same length, the triangle is called equilateral. Then all three angles are equal too.
70287.m: An equilateral triangle has three sides of equal length.

70288.q: How big is each angle in an equilateral triangle?
70288.e: All three angles are equal, so 180° ÷ 3 gives 60°.
70288.m: In an equilateral triangle each angle measures 60 degrees.

70289.q: What is the longest side of a right-angled triangle called?
70289.e: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is always the longest side. The other two sides are called catheti or legs.
70289.m: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.

70290.q: What are the two equal sides of an isosceles triangle called?
70290.e: The two equal sides are called legs, and the third side is called the base.
70290.m: An isosceles triangle has two legs of equal length.

70291.q: A triangle has the angles 30°, 50° and 100°. What is it called?
70291.e: One angle is greater than 90°, namely 100°. That is why the triangle is obtuse-angled.
70291.m: A triangle with an obtuse angle is called obtuse-angled.

70292.q: A triangle has the angles 50°, 60° and 70°. What is it called?
70292.e: All three angles are less than 90°. Such a triangle is called acute-angled.
70292.m: If all the angles are acute, the triangle is acute-angled.

70293.q: With which three side lengths can you make a triangle?
70293.e: Any two sides together must always be longer than the third. Only with 4 + 5 = 9 cm, which is longer than 7 cm, does it work.
70293.m: Two sides of a triangle together are always longer than the third side.

70294.q: What is a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides called?
70294.e: A trapezium has two parallel opposite sides. A parallelogram and a rectangle have two pairs.
70294.m: A trapezium has two sides that are parallel to each other.

70295.q: What is a quadrilateral made of two pairs of equal, neighbouring sides called?
70295.e: In a kite, two equal sides meet each other twice. It looks like a kite you fly.
70295.m: A kite has two pairs of equal neighbouring sides.

70296.q: What is a quadrilateral called whose opposite sides are parallel but which has no right angles?
70296.e: In a parallelogram both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. The angles do not have to be right angles.
70296.m: In a parallelogram the opposite sides are parallel and of equal length.

70297.q: What is true of the two diagonals in every rectangle?
a: They are always perpendicular to each other.
They are parallel to each other.
They are as long as the sides.
70297.e: In a rectangle the diagonals are the same length and bisect each other. They are only perpendicular in a square.
70297.m: The diagonals of a rectangle are the same length.

70298.q: In which quadrilateral are the diagonals always perpendicular to each other?
70298.e: In a rhombus the diagonals always cross at a right angle and bisect each other.
70298.m: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular to each other.

70299.q: In a parallelogram one angle measures 70°. How big is a neighbouring angle?
70299.e: Neighbouring angles in a parallelogram add up to 180°. So 180° minus 70° gives 110°.
70299.m: In a parallelogram two neighbouring angles add up to 180 degrees.

70300.q: A rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
70300.e: The perimeter is 2 times 9 cm plus 2 times 4 cm, so 18 cm + 8 cm gives 26 cm.
70300.m: You get the perimeter of a rectangle by adding all four sides.

70301.q: A square has a side length of 7.5 cm. What is its perimeter?
70301.e: A square has four sides of equal length: 4 times 7.5 cm gives 30 cm.
70301.m: The perimeter of a square is four times as long as one side.

70302.q: An equilateral triangle has a side length of 8 cm. What is its perimeter?
70302.e: All three sides are 8 cm long: 3 times 8 cm gives 24 cm.
70302.m: The perimeter is the length of the whole outline of a shape.

70303.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 m and is 9 m long. How wide is it?
70303.e: Length and width together are half the perimeter, so 15 m. The width is 15 m minus 9 m, which gives 6 m.
70303.m: The length and width of a rectangle together make half the perimeter.

70304.q: A farmer puts a fence round a rectangular field 40 m long and 25 m wide. How many metres of fence does she need?
70304.e: The fence goes all the way round: 2 times 40 m + 2 times 25 m gives 80 m + 50 m, so 130 m.
70304.m: For a fence round an area, you need a length equal to the perimeter.

70305.q: A triangle has the sides 5 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. What is its perimeter?
70305.e: You add all three sides: 5 cm + 7 cm + 9 cm gives 21 cm.
70305.m: For the perimeter of a triangle, you add all three sides.

70306.q: Which formula gives the perimeter of a rectangle with length a and width b?
70306.e: A rectangle has two sides of length a and two sides of length b. a · b would be the area.
70306.m: The perimeter of a rectangle is twice the length plus twice the width.

70307.q: A room is 5 m long and 4 m wide. What is its floor area?
70307.e: The area of a rectangle is length times width: 5 m times 4 m gives 20 m².
70307.m: The area of a rectangle is length times width.

70308.q: A square has a side length of 9 cm. What is its area?
70308.e: For a square you work out side times side: 9 cm times 9 cm gives 81 cm². 36 cm would be the perimeter.
70308.m: The area of a square is side times side.

70309.q: A rectangle has an area of 48 cm² and is 8 cm long. How wide is it?
70309.e: Width is area divided by length: 48 cm² ÷ 8 cm gives 6 cm.
70309.m: If you know the area and length, you divide the area by the length.

70310.q: A right-angled triangle has the two shorter sides (catheti) 6 cm and 8 cm. What is its area?
70310.e: The triangle is half a rectangle of 6 cm by 8 cm. 48 cm² ÷ 2 gives 24 cm².
70310.m: A right-angled triangle is half the size of the matching rectangle.

70311.q: A triangle has a base of 9 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area?
70311.e: Area is base times height divided by 2: 9 cm times 4 cm gives 36 cm², halved 18 cm².
70311.m: The area of a triangle is base times height divided by two.

70312.q: A parallelogram has a base of 7 cm and a height of 5 cm. What is its area?
70312.e: For a parallelogram you work out base times height: 7 cm times 5 cm gives 35 cm². You must not use the slanting side.
70312.m: The area of a parallelogram is base times height.

70313.q: The length and width of a rectangle are doubled. How does the area change?
70313.e: The new area is 2a times 2b, so 4 times a times b. The area quadruples.
70313.m: If you double all the sides, the area becomes four times as big.

70314.q: A bathroom floor is 3.5 m long and 2 m wide. How many square metres of tiles do you need?
70314.e: 3.5 m times 2 m gives 7 m². 11 m would be the perimeter.
70314.m: For floor coverings, you work out the area of the floor.

70315.q: Which Greek letter is used for the circle number?
70315.e: The circle number is called pi and is written with the Greek letter π.
70315.m: The circle number is called pi.

70316.q: What does the number π tell you?
70316.e: For every circle, the circumference divided by the diameter gives the same number, namely π.
70316.m: For every circle, the circumference is about 3.14 times as long as the diameter.

70317.q: A circle has a circumference of 62.8 cm. How long is its radius if you use π = 3.14?
70317.e: The diameter is 62.8 cm ÷ 3.14, so 20 cm. The radius is half of that, so 10 cm.
70317.m: You get the diameter from the circumference by dividing by pi.

70318.q: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. About how long is its circumference?
70318.e: Circumference is π times diameter: 3.14 times 10 cm gives 31.4 cm.
70318.m: The circumference of a circle is a bit more than three times the diameter.

70319.q: A circle has a radius of 3 cm. What is its circumference if you use π = 3.14?
70319.e: The diameter is 6 cm. 3.14 times 6 cm gives 18.84 cm.
70319.m: With the radius, you must first double it to get the diameter.

70320.q: A bike wheel has a diameter of 70 cm. About how far does the bike roll in one turn of the wheel?
70320.e: In one turn the wheel rolls out its circumference: 3.14 times 70 cm gives about 220 cm, so about 2.2 m.
70320.m: In one turn a wheel rolls exactly its circumference.

70321.q: Which fraction is a well-known approximation for π?
70321.e: 22 divided by 7 gives about 3.143, which is very close to π at 3.1416.
70321.m: The fraction 22 sevenths is a good approximation for pi.

70322.q: On which date do maths fans celebrate Pi Day?
70322.e: In the American way of writing dates, 14 March is written as 3/14, which is a reminder of 3.14.
70322.m: Pi Day is celebrated every year on 14 March.

70323.q: How many different nets of a cube are there?
70323.e: There are exactly 11 different cube nets, if rotated and mirrored nets are not counted twice.
70323.m: There are eleven different nets for a cube.

70324.q: A cube has an edge length of 2 cm. What is its surface area?
70324.e: Each of the 6 faces measures 2 cm by 2 cm, so 4 cm². 6 times 4 cm² gives 24 cm².
70324.m: The surface of a cube is made of six identical squares.

70325.q: In a cube net, what is the largest number of squares in one straight row?
70325.e: Four squares in a row form the side walls all the way round. A fifth in the same row would overlap the first.
70325.m: In a cube net there are never more than four squares in a row.

70326.q: How many faces meet at each corner of a cube?
70326.e: At each corner of a cube, three faces and three edges meet.
70326.m: Three faces meet at each corner of a cube.

70327.q: How many edges of a cuboid are exactly as long as its height?
70327.e: A cuboid has 12 edges in three directions. Each set of 4 edges points the same way and is the same length, so there are 4 vertical edges.
70327.m: In a cuboid, four edges are always parallel and of equal length.

70328.q: A cuboid is 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2 cm high. What is its volume?
70328.e: 8 cm times 5 cm times 2 cm gives 80 cm³.
70328.m: Volume is given in cubic units such as cubic centimetres.

70329.q: A cube-shaped box measures 10 cm by 10 cm by 10 cm inside. How much fits into it?
70329.e: 10 cm times 10 cm times 10 cm gives 1000 cm³. That is one cubic decimetre, so exactly 1 litre.
70329.m: One cubic decimetre holds exactly one litre.

70330.q: A cuboid has a volume of 120 cm³ and a base of 4 cm by 5 cm. How high is it?
70330.e: The base area is 20 cm². The height is 120 cm³ ÷ 20 cm², which gives 6 cm.
70330.m: The height of a cuboid is the volume divided by the base area.

70331.q: A swimming pool is 25 m long, 10 m wide and 2 m deep. How much water does it hold?
70331.e: 25 m times 10 m times 2 m gives 500 m³. That is 500,000 litres.
70331.m: A large pool is measured in cubic metres.

70332.q: How many cubic millimetres are there in a cubic centimetre?
70332.e: 1 cm is 10 mm. 10 times 10 times 10 gives 1000 mm³.
70332.m: For units of volume, the conversion number is 1000.

70333.q: How many centimetre cubes fit into a cuboid 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high?
70333.e: One layer holds 4 times 3, which gives 12 cubes. There are 2 layers, so 24 cubes.
70333.m: Volume counts how many unit cubes fit into a solid.

70334.q: A sandpit is 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and is filled with sand 30 cm deep. How much sand do you need?
70334.e: 30 cm is 0.3 m. 2 m times 1.5 m times 0.3 m gives 0.9 m³.
70334.m: Before calculating, all lengths must be in the same unit.

70335.q: How many lines of symmetry does an equilateral triangle have?
70335.e: Each line from a corner to the middle of the opposite side is a line of symmetry. That gives three lines.
70335.m: An equilateral triangle has three lines of symmetry.

70336.q: How many lines of symmetry does an isosceles triangle have if it is not equilateral?
70336.e: The only line of symmetry goes through the top and the middle of the base.
70336.m: An isosceles triangle has one line of symmetry.

70337.q: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have if it is not a square?
70337.e: The two centre lines are lines of symmetry. The diagonals are not lines of symmetry in a rectangle, only in a square.
70337.m: A rectangle has two lines of symmetry through the middles of its sides.

70338.q: In a reflection, what is true of a point and its image?
a: They are the same distance from the mirror line.
The image is twice as far away.
Both are on the same side of the mirror line.
The image is always on the mirror line.
70338.e: The line joining the point and its image is perpendicular to the mirror line, and both are the same distance from it.
70338.m: In a reflection, the point and its image are the same distance from the mirror line.

70339.q: What is the smallest angle you must turn a square through so that it fits exactly onto itself again?
70339.e: A square has four equal corners. 360° ÷ 4 gives 90°.
70339.m: A square has rotational symmetry with an angle of 90 degrees.

70340.q: What is the smallest angle you must turn an equilateral triangle through so that it lies on itself again?
70340.e: The triangle has three equal corners. 360° ÷ 3 gives 120°.
70340.m: You get the smallest angle of rotation of a regular shape from 360 degrees divided by the number of corners.

70341.q: Which capital letter has rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry?
70341.e: S looks the same after a half turn of 180°, but has no mirror line. A, E and T have a mirror line.
70341.m: A shape can have rotational symmetry without having a line of symmetry.

70342.q: What rotational symmetry does every parallelogram have?
70342.e: If you turn a parallelogram 180° about the point where the diagonals cross, it lies on itself again.

70343.q: What is the smallest angle of rotation of a regular pentagon?
70343.e: A regular pentagon has five equal corners. 360° ÷ 5 gives 72°.
70343.m: A regular pentagon fits onto itself again after a turn of 72 degrees.

70344.q: Which of these shapes does NOT have rotational symmetry?
70344.e: A rectangle and a rhombus fit onto themselves again after a half turn, a regular hexagon after only 60°. An isosceles trapezium only has line symmetry.
70344.m: Not every shape with line symmetry also has rotational symmetry.

70345.q: What is the smallest angle of rotation of a regular hexagon?
70345.e: A regular hexagon has six equal corners. 360° ÷ 6 gives 60°.
70345.m: A regular hexagon has rotational symmetry with an angle of 60 degrees.

70346.q: Which sign do you use to write that two straight lines are parallel?
70346.e: The sign ∥ is made of two parallel strokes. g ∥ h is read “g is parallel to h”.
70346.m: Two upright strokes are the sign for parallel.

70347.q: How many points of intersection do two different parallel lines have?
70347.e: Parallel lines are the same distance apart everywhere. That is why they never cross.

70348.q: Line g is parallel to h, and h is parallel to k. How are g and k positioned in relation to each other?
70348.e: If two lines are parallel to the same third line, they are also parallel to each other.
70348.m: Two lines parallel to the same line are also parallel to each other.

70349.q: A straight line crosses two parallel lines. What are the equal angles called that are in the same position at both crossing points?
70349.e: Corresponding angles are on the same side and in the same position at the two crossing points. With parallel lines they are equal.
70349.m: With parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal.

70350.q: Which sign do you use to write that two straight lines are perpendicular?
70350.e: The sign ⊥ shows a right angle. g ⊥ h is read “g is perpendicular to h”.
70350.m: The sign for perpendicular looks like an upside-down T.

70351.q: What do you call two straight lines that cross at a right angle?
70351.e: If two lines cross at 90°, they are perpendicular to each other. This is also called orthogonal.
70351.m: Perpendicular lines cross at a right angle.

70352.q: How do you measure the shortest distance from a point to a straight line?
a: along the perpendicular to the line
at a 45° angle to the line
70352.e: The shortest way from a point to a straight line is always the perpendicular. Any slanting way is longer.
70352.m: Distances are always measured at right angles.

70353.q: Line g is perpendicular to h, and h is perpendicular to k. All lie in the same plane. How are g and k positioned in relation to each other?
70353.e: g and k both make a right angle with h. In a plane they are therefore parallel to each other.
70353.m: Two perpendiculars to the same line are parallel in a plane.

70354.q: What is the line called that you drop at right angles from a point onto a straight line?
70354.e: The perpendicular is the line at right angles from a point to a straight line. The point where it meets the line is called the foot of the perpendicular.
70354.m: A perpendicular is at right angles to the line.

70355.q: Where is the point (4, 0) in the coordinate system?
70355.e: The y-coordinate is 0. So the point is neither above nor below the x-axis, but on it.
70355.m: Points with a y-coordinate of zero lie on the x-axis.

70356.q: In which quadrant is the point (-2, -6)?
70356.e: Both coordinates are negative, so the point is at the bottom left. That is the 3rd quadrant.
70356.m: In the third quadrant both coordinates are negative.

70357.q: The point A(2, 5) is moved 3 units to the right and 4 units down. Where is it then?
70357.e: To the right, the x-coordinate gets bigger: 2 + 3 gives 5. Downwards, the y-coordinate gets smaller: 5 minus 4 gives 1.
70357.m: When moving a point, you change x for left and right and y for up and down.

70358.q: A rectangle has the corners (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 4) and (1, 4). What is its area?
70358.e: The length is 5 minus 1, which gives 4; the height is 4 minus 1, which gives 3. The area is 4 times 3, so 12.
70358.m: You get side lengths in the coordinate system as the difference of the coordinates.

70359.q: The point (3, 2) is reflected in the y-axis. Where is the image?
70359.e: When reflecting in the y-axis, only the x-coordinate changes its sign.
70359.m: When reflecting in the y-axis, the x-coordinate changes its sign.

70360.q: Which mathematician is the Cartesian coordinate system named after?
70360.e: The Cartesian coordinate system is named after the French mathematician René Descartes, Cartesius in Latin.
70360.m: The Cartesian coordinate system bears the name of René Descartes.

70361.q: On a map with a scale of 1 : 25,000, two places are 4 cm apart. How far is that in reality?
70361.e: 4 cm times 25,000 gives 100,000 cm. That is 1000 m, so 1 km.
70361.m: With the scale you convert map distances into real distances.

70362.q: What does the scale 1 : 50,000 mean on a map?
a: 1 cm on the map is 500 m in reality.
1 cm on the map is 50 m in reality.
1 cm on the map is 5 km in reality.
1 cm on the map is 50 km in reality.
70362.e: 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm long in reality. That is 500 m.
70362.m: At a scale of 1 to 50,000, everything is shown 50,000 times smaller.

70363.q: A room is 4.5 m long. How long is it drawn on a plan with a scale of 1 : 100?
70363.e: 4.5 m is 450 cm. 450 cm ÷ 100 gives 4.5 cm.
70363.m: At a scale of 1 to 100, each metre is drawn as one centimetre.

70364.q: A hike is 3 km long. How long is the route on a map with a scale of 1 : 50,000?
70364.m: For the map distance, you divide the real distance by the scale number.

70365.q: A beetle is drawn at a scale of 5 : 1. The drawing is 2 cm long. How long is the real beetle?
70365.e: The drawing is enlarged 5 times. 2 cm ÷ 5 gives 0.4 cm, so 4 mm.
70365.m: If the bigger number comes first, the drawing is an enlargement.

70366.q: Which national map shows the most detail?
70366.e: The smaller the scale number, the less things are reduced and the more detail there is room for. swisstopo publishes national maps at scales including 1 : 25,000.
70366.m: The smaller the scale number, the more detailed the map.

70367.q: A real distance of 2 km is 8 cm long on a map. What is the scale of the map?
70367.m: You find the scale by dividing the real distance by the map distance.

70368.q: A model car at a scale of 1 : 43 is 10 cm long. How long is the real car?
70368.e: 10 cm times 43 gives 430 cm, so 4.3 m.
70368.m: For the real length, you multiply the model length by the scale number.

70369.q: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
70369.e: Three lines go through opposite corners, three more through the middles of opposite sides. That is 6 altogether.
70369.m: A regular hexagon has six lines of symmetry.

70370.q: What is a flat shape called that can be folded up into a solid?
70370.e: A net shows all the faces of a solid joined together in a plane. If you fold it along the edges, you get the solid.
70370.m: A net can be folded into the solid.

70371.q: 3 croissants cost 4.50 francs. How much do 7 croissants cost?
70371.e: One croissant costs 4.50 ÷ 3 = 1.50 francs. 7 croissants cost 7 · 1.50 = 10.50 francs.
70371.m: With the unitary method, you first work back to one unit.

70372.q: 5 kg of apples cost 17.50 francs. How much do 2 kg of apples cost?
70372.e: 1 kg costs 17.50 ÷ 5 = 3.50 francs. 2 kg cost 2 · 3.50 = 7.00 francs.
70372.m: The price for one kilogram helps you calculate any amount.

70373.q: A car uses 28 litres of petrol for 400 km. How much does it use for 250 km?
70373.e: Per kilometre the car uses 28 ÷ 400 = 0.07 litres. For 250 km it is 250 · 0.07 = 17.5 litres.
70373.m: You find the consumption for a shorter distance from the consumption per kilometre.

70374.q: With 12 litres of paint you can paint 90 m² of wall. How many m² can you paint with 20 litres?
70374.e: With 1 litre you paint 90 ÷ 12 = 7.5 m². With 20 litres it is 20 · 7.5 = 150 m².
70374.m: More paint is enough for a correspondingly larger area.

70375.q: 8 exercise books cost 14.40 francs. How much do 5 exercise books cost?
70375.e: One exercise book costs 14.40 ÷ 8 = 1.80 francs. 5 exercise books cost 5 · 1.80 = 9.00 francs.
70375.m: If you know the price of one, you can work out any total price.

70376.q: A tap fills 27 litres in 3 minutes. How many litres is that in 8 minutes?
70376.e: In 1 minute, 27 ÷ 3 = 9 litres flow. In 8 minutes it is 8 · 9 = 72 litres.
70376.m: Steady flow can be worked out with the unitary method.

70377.q: In the unitary method (rule of three), what do you work out in the middle step?
a: The final value for the amount you want
The difference between the two amounts
The average of all the values
70377.e: The rule of three has three steps: the starting statement, working back to one unit and working forward to the amount you want. In the middle step you find the value for one unit.
70377.m: The rule of three goes via one unit to the value you want.

70378.q: 250 g of cheese cost 6 francs. How much does 1 kg of this cheese cost?
70378.e: 1 kg is 1000 g, so four times 250 g. The price is therefore 4 · 6 = 24 francs.
70378.m: One kilogram is four times 250 grams.

70379.q: At an assumed exchange rate, 100 euros cost 94 francs. How many francs do 250 euros cost?
70379.e: 1 euro costs 0.94 francs. 250 euros cost 250 · 0.94 = 235 francs.
70379.m: When changing money, you use the rate like a price per unit.

70380.q: What does the graph of a direct proportion look like?
a: A straight line through the origin
A straight line that does not go through the origin
70380.e: In a direct proportion, x = 0 goes with y = 0, and y grows steadily with x. That is why all the points lie on a straight line through the origin.
70380.m: Direct proportions give a straight line through the origin.

70381.q: Each of x = 1, 2, 3 has a y-value. Which y-values fit a direct proportion?
70381.e: With 4, 8, 12, y is always four times x. In the other rows, y divided by x is not always the same.
70381.m: With directly proportional values, y is always the same multiple of x.

70382.q: In a direct proportion, what is the same for all pairs of values?
a: The quotient y divided by x
70382.e: In direct proportions, y divided by x is always the same. This number is called the constant of proportionality.
70382.m: The constant of proportionality is the same for all pairs of values.

70383.q: In a table of direct proportion, x = 4 goes with y = 10. Which value goes with x = 10?
70383.e: The factor is 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. So x = 10 goes with 10 · 2.5 = 25.
70383.m: With the factor of a table, you can fill in all the missing values.

a: Amount of minced meat and price at a fixed price per kilo
Age and height of a child
Time of day and outside temperature
Number of painters and length of the job
70384.e: At a fixed price per kilo, twice the amount costs twice as much. Age and height or time and temperature do not grow steadily together.
70384.m: A relationship is only proportional if double always gives double.

70385.q: In a direct proportion, x is tripled. What happens to y?
70385.e: With proportionality, x and y change in the same ratio. If x is multiplied by 3, y is also multiplied by 3.
70385.m: With proportional quantities, both change in the same ratio.

70386.q: A taxi ride costs a basic fee of 6 francs plus 3 francs per kilometre. Is the price proportional to the distance?
a: No, because of the basic fee
Yes, because each kilometre costs the same
Yes, because the price rises with the distance
No, because the price falls with the distance
70386.e: For 1 km you pay 9 francs, but for 2 km only 12 francs and not 18 francs. Because of the basic fee, the price does not double with the distance.
70386.m: A fixed basic fee stops a price from being proportional.

70387.q: For a relationship, y = 2.5 · x. Which y-value goes with x = 8?
70387.m: In the equation of a direct proportion, the factor comes before the x.

70388.q: 4 workers need 15 days to build a wall. How long do 6 workers who work just as fast need?
70388.e: The whole job is 4 · 15 = 60 working days. So 6 workers need 60 ÷ 6 = 10 days.
70388.m: More workers need less time for the same job.

70389.q: In an inverse proportion, what stays the same for all pairs of values?
a: The quotient y divided by x
70389.e: If x is doubled, y is halved. That is why the product x times y always stays the same.
70389.m: In inverse proportion, the product of the pairs of values is constant.

70390.q: What is the curve called that an inverse proportion makes in the coordinate system?
70390.e: The points lie on a curved line that gets closer and closer to the axes but never touches them. This curve is called a hyperbola.

70391.q: A supply of feed lasts 8 horses for 30 days. How long does it last for 12 horses?
70391.e: The supply is enough for 8 · 30 = 240 horse days. For 12 horses it lasts 240 ÷ 12 = 20 days.
70391.m: More eaters empty a supply faster.

70392.q: A journey takes exactly 3 hours at 60 km/h. How long does it take at 90 km/h?
70392.e: The distance is 60 · 3 = 180 km. At 90 km/h it takes 180 ÷ 90 = 2 hours.
70392.m: For the same distance, the journey time falls when the speed rises.

70393.q: In an inverse proportion, x is halved. What happens to y?
70393.e: Because the product x times y must stay the same, y becomes twice as big when x becomes half as big.
70393.m: If you halve one quantity, the other doubles.

a: Number of people and share of a pizza per person
Amount of petrol and price at the petrol station
Side length and perimeter of a square
Number of tickets and total price
70394.e: If twice as many people share the same pizza, each one only gets half. The other examples are directly proportional.
70394.m: When sharing fairly, everyone gets less if more people join in.

70395.q: A rectangle must always have an area of 36 cm². How long is it if it is 3 cm wide?
70395.e: Length times width gives 36 cm². So the length is 36 ÷ 3 = 12 cm.
70395.m: For the same area, a rectangle gets longer when it gets narrower.

70397.m: One tonne equals a thousand kilograms.

70398.m: To convert grams into kilograms, you divide by a thousand.

70400.q: How many grams are there in a tonne?
70400.m: A tonne has a million grams.

70401.q: How many centimetres do 5 dm and 30 cm make together?
70401.e: 5 dm is 50 cm. 50 cm + 30 cm = 80 cm.
70401.m: Before adding, all lengths must be in the same unit.

70402.q: How many milligrams are there in a gram?
70402.e: Milli means one thousandth. That is why a gram has 1000 milligrams.
70402.m: A milligram is a thousandth of a gram.

70403.q: Which prefix for units of measurement means “one hundredth”?
70403.e: A centimetre is a hundredth of a metre. Deci means one tenth and milli one thousandth.
70403.m: The prefix centi stands for one hundredth.

70404.q: How many metres are 0.6 km and 450 m together?
70404.m: You change kilometres into metres by multiplying by a thousand.

70405.q: A cyclist covers 36 km in 2 hours. What is her average speed?
70405.e: Speed is distance divided by time: 36 km ÷ 2 h = 18 km/h.
70405.m: Average speed shows how far you travel per hour.

70406.q: How many metres per second are 36 km/h?
70406.m: One metre per second is faster than one kilometre per hour.

70407.m: To get km/h, you multiply a speed in m/s by 3.6.

70408.q: A train travels at 120 km/h. How far does it get in 45 minutes?
70408.m: The distance is speed times time.

70409.q: A hiker walks at 4.5 km/h. How long does she take for 18 km?
70409.e: Time is distance divided by speed: 18 ÷ 4.5 = 4 hours.
70409.m: You get the time by dividing the distance by the speed.

70410.q: A cyclist rides at 12 km/h. How many minutes does he take for 1 km?
70410.e: In 60 minutes he rides 12 km. So for 1 km he needs 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes.
70410.m: If you know the speed, you can work out the time for one kilometre.

70411.q: What is the general speed limit on Swiss motorways?
70411.e: On Swiss motorways you may generally drive at no more than 120 km/h, unless a lower limit is signposted.
70411.m: On Swiss motorways the general limit is 120.

70412.q: Sound travels about 340 m per second in air. 3 seconds pass between the lightning and the thunder. About how far away is the storm?
70412.e: In 3 seconds sound travels about 3 · 340 = 1020 m. That is about 1 km.
70412.m: Three seconds between lightning and thunder mean a distance of about one kilometre.

70413.q: A train leaves at 8.47 and arrives at 10.12. How long is the journey?
70413.e: From 8.47 to 9.47 is 1 hour. From 9.47 to 10.12 there are another 25 minutes.
70413.m: Journey times are easiest to work out in steps over full hours.

70414.q: From 6.05 a bus leaves every 15 minutes. When does the fifth bus leave?
70414.e: The buses leave at 6.05, 6.20, 6.35, 6.50 and 7.05. So the fifth bus leaves at 7.05.
70414.m: For the first bus, no 15 minutes are added yet.

70415.q: How many minutes are 2 hours and 15 minutes?

70416.q: How many seconds are there in an hour?
70416.e: An hour has 60 minutes, each with 60 seconds. 60 · 60 = 3600 seconds.
70416.m: An hour has three thousand six hundred seconds.

70417.q: A night train leaves at 23.40 and travels for 50 minutes. When does it arrive?
70417.e: It is 20 minutes to midnight. The remaining 30 minutes take you to 0.30.
70417.m: After 24:00 the time starts again at 0:00.

70418.q: In a regular-interval timetable, a train leaves every hour at the same minute. The first leaves at 6.07. When does the fourth train leave?
70418.e: The trains leave at 6.07, 7.07, 8.07 and 9.07. So the fourth train leaves at 9.07.
70418.m: In a regular-interval timetable, trains leave at regular intervals at the same minute.

70419.q: A film starts at 19.35 and lasts 128 minutes. When does it end?
70419.e: 128 minutes are 2 hours and 8 minutes. 19.35 plus 2 h 8 min gives 21.43.
70419.m: You split long periods of time into hours and minutes.

70420.q: Lea has the marks 5, 4.5, 6 and 4.5. What is her average mark?
70420.e: The sum is 5 + 4.5 + 6 + 4.5 = 20. Divided by 4 marks, that gives 5.
70420.m: For the average, you divide the sum by the number of values.

70421.q: On five days, 12, 15, 9, 14 and 10 degrees are measured. What is the average temperature?
70421.m: The mean evens out high and low values.

70422.q: The average of 4 numbers is 8. What is their sum?
70422.e: Average times number of values gives the sum: 8 · 4 = 32.
70422.m: From the mean and the number of values, you can work out the sum.

70423.q: The mean of 4 numbers is 6. Now the number 11 is added. What is the new mean?
70423.e: The 4 numbers have the sum 4 · 6 = 24. With the 11 the sum is 35, and 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
70423.m: A new value above the mean raises the mean.

70424.q: Which measure is changed especially strongly by a single extremely large value?
70424.e: In the arithmetic mean, every value goes into the sum with its full size. That is why an outlier moves the average a lot.
70424.m: Outliers can badly distort an average.

70425.q: What is the mean of the numbers -3, 5, 7 and -1?
70425.e: The sum is -3 + 5 + 7 + (-1) = 8. Divided by 4, that gives 2.
70425.m: Negative numbers also count with their sign in the mean.

70426.q: A cyclist rides 42 km, 35 km and 49 km on three days. How many kilometres does he ride per day on average?
70426.m: The daily average is the total distance divided by the number of days.

70427.q: The mean of three numbers is 10. Two of the numbers are 8 and 9. What is the third number?
70427.e: The sum of the three numbers is 3 · 10 = 30. Missing: 30 minus 8 minus 9 = 13.
70427.m: You find missing values using the sum of all the values.

70428.q: What is the median of the values 2, 8, 4 and 10?
70428.e: In order, the list is 2, 4, 8, 10. With an even number of values you take the mean of the two middle values: (4 + 8) ÷ 2 = 6.
70428.m: With an even number of values, the median is between the two middle values.

70429.q: What is the median of a set of data?
a: The value in the middle of the ordered list
The most common value in the list
The sum divided by the number of values
The difference between the largest and smallest value
70429.e: You put all the values in order of size. The value exactly in the middle is the median.
70429.m: For the median, you must first put the values in order of size.

70430.q: What is the median of the values 12, 3, 7, 3, 20, 9 and 5?
70430.e: In order: 3, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 20. With 7 values, the 7 is in fourth place.
70430.m: With an odd number of values, the median is exactly one value in the list.

70431.q: An ordered list has 9 values. In which place is the median?
70431.e: Before the 5th value there are 4 values and after it there are also 4 values. So it is exactly in the middle.
70431.m: With an odd number of values, there is exactly one middle value.

70432.q: Five monthly wages are 4000, 4200, 4500, 4800 and 30,000 francs. What is the median?
70432.e: The values are already in order; the middle one is 4500 francs. Because of the very high wage, the mean would be 9500 francs.
70432.m: With wages, the median often tells you more than the average.

70433.q: The ordered values are 2, 4, x, 10, 12 and 15. The median is 8. What is x?
70433.e: The two middle values are x and 10. Their mean is 8, so x + 10 = 16 and x = 6.
70433.m: You can work back to a missing middle value from the median.

70434.q: What is the median of the values 1.5, 2.5, 4, 6, 6 and 7?
70434.e: The list is in order and has 6 values. The middle values are 4 and 6, so (4 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5.
70434.m: You find the median of an ordered list by working in from both ends.

70435.q: The number 20 is added to the values 4, 6 and 9. How does the median change?
70435.e: Before, 6 is the middle value. With 4, 6, 9, 20 there are four values; the middle ones are 6 and 9, so (6 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7.5.
70435.m: An extra value can move the median, even if it changes it only a little.

70436.q: What is a chart with upright rectangles called?
70436.e: In a column chart the rectangles stand upright like columns. If they lie horizontally, it is called a bar chart.
70436.m: Columns stand upright, bars lie horizontally.

70437.q: In a pie chart, one sector is 72°. What proportion is that?
70437.e: The whole circle has 360°. 72 ÷ 360 = 0.2, which is 20 %.
70437.m: In a pie chart, 360 degrees stand for the whole.

70438.q: Which type of chart shows how often values occur that are grouped into classes such as 0 to 10 kg, 10 to 20 kg?
70438.e: A histogram uses rectangles that touch each other to show how many values are in each class.
70438.m: A histogram shows the frequencies of classes.

70439.q: Which type of chart is suitable for showing the link between height and weight of many people?
70439.e: In a scatter graph, each person is plotted as a point with two values. This lets you see whether the quantities are linked.
70439.m: A scatter graph shows how two features are linked.

70440.q: What does a box plot show besides the minimum and maximum?
70440.e: A box plot shows the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum. The box covers the middle half of the values.
70440.m: The box of a box plot contains the middle half of the data.

70441.q: In a pictogram, one bike symbol stands for 50 bikes. How many bikes do 3.5 symbols show?
70441.e: 3.5 · 50 = 175. The half symbol stands for 25 bikes.
70441.m: In a pictogram you must always check what one symbol stands for.

70442.q: Why can a column chart be misleading if the y-axis does not start at 0?
a: Differences look bigger than they are
The columns all become the same height
The values are added up wrongly
The order of the columns changes
70442.e: If you cut off the bottom part of the axis, small differences between the columns look very large.
70442.m: With charts, it is always worth looking at the axis labels.

70443.q: What is a chart with horizontal rectangles called?
70443.e: In a bar chart the rectangles lie horizontally. It works well when the labels are long.
70443.m: Long labels fit well next to horizontal bars.

70444.q: A spinner has 8 equal sections, 3 of which are red. What is the probability of red?
70444.e: There are 3 favourable sections out of 8 possible, equally likely sections. The probability is 3/8.
70444.m: Probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the number of possible outcomes.

70445.q: What probability does a certain event have?
70445.e: A certain event always happens. Its probability is 1, which is 100 %.

70446.q: There are 200 tickets in a raffle drum, 10 of which win. What is the probability of winning with one ticket?
70446.e: 10 out of 200 tickets win. 10 ÷ 200 = 0.05, which is 5 %.
70446.m: Probabilities can also be given in per cent.

70447.q: A pack of Jass cards (a Swiss card game) has 36 cards with 4 aces. What is the probability of drawing an ace without looking?
70447.e: There are 4 aces among 36 cards. 4/36 simplified gives 1/9.
70447.m: Fractions in probability are simplified like other fractions.

70448.q: What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4 with a dice?
70448.e: Only 5 and 6 are greater than 4. That is 2 out of 6 outcomes, so 1/3.
70448.m: For probabilities, you first count all the favourable outcomes.

70449.q: You roll a fair dice 600 times. About how often do you expect a 3?
70449.m: With many trials, the relative frequency gets close to the probability.

70450.q: What is true of a Laplace experiment?
a: The outcomes depend on each other
70450.e: A Laplace experiment has outcomes that are all equally likely, as with a fair dice or a coin.
70450.m: A fair dice is a typical Laplace experiment.

70451.q: The probability of rain is 0.3. What is the probability that it does not rain?
70451.e: An event and its opposite add up to 1. 1 minus 0.3 = 0.7.
70451.m: The probability of the opposite event makes a probability up to 1.

70452.q: You roll two dice. What is the probability of a double (two equal numbers)?
70452.e: There are 36 equally likely outcomes, 6 of which are doubles (1 and 1 up to 6 and 6). 6/36 = 1/6.
70452.m: With two dice there are thirty-six possible outcomes.

70453.q: How many two-digit numbers can you make with the digits 1 to 5 if digits may be repeated?
70453.e: There are 5 choices for the tens place and again 5 for the ones place. 5 · 5 = 25 numbers, including 11 or 55, for example.
70453.m: If digits may repeat, the choice stays the same at every place.

70454.q: Mia has 3 T-shirts and 4 pairs of trousers. How many different combinations can she wear?
70454.e: Each T-shirt goes with 4 pairs of trousers. 3 · 4 = 12 combinations.

70455.q: A combination lock has 3 wheels with the digits 0 to 9. How many codes are there?
70455.e: Each wheel has 10 options. 10 · 10 · 10 = 1000 codes, from 000 to 999.
70455.m: Each extra wheel multiplies the number of codes by ten.

70456.q: Which diagram shows all the possibilities of a multi-step choice clearly as branches?
70456.e: In a tree diagram, each step branches into its possibilities. Every path from start to finish is one possible combination.
70456.m: A tree diagram helps you count systematically.

70457.q: A menu offers a choice of 2 starters, 3 main courses and 2 desserts. How many different menus are there?
70457.m: With several steps of choice, you multiply the number of possibilities at each step.

70458.m: The factorial is the product of all natural numbers up to that number.

70459.q: A team of two is picked from 6 children. How many different teams are possible?
70459.e: For ordered pairs there would be 6 · 5 = 30 possibilities. Since the order in the team does not matter, there are 30 : 2 = 15.
70459.m: If the order does not matter, you divide by the number of arrangements.

70460.q: 5 runners start a race. In how many ways can gold, silver and bronze be awarded?
70460.e: There are 5 possibilities for gold, then 4 for silver and 3 for bronze. 5 · 4 · 3 = 60.
70460.m: When order matters, the choice shrinks with every place awarded.

70461.q: How many ares are there in a hectare?
70461.e: An are is 100 m² and a hectare is 10,000 m². 10,000 : 100 = 100 ares.
70461.m: A hectare is made up of a hundred ares.

70462.q: How many hectares are there in a square kilometre?
70462.e: 1 km² is 1000 m · 1000 m = 1,000,000 m². Divided by 10,000 m² per hectare, that gives 100 ha.
70462.m: With units of area, the conversion step is often a hundred.

70463.q: How many square decimetres are 3.5 m²?
70463.m: Between neighbouring units of area there is a factor of a hundred.

70464.q: A building plot measures 2400 m². How many ares is that?
70464.m: An are is the area of a square ten metres by ten metres.

70466.q: How many litres are there in a hectolitre?
70466.e: The prefix hecto means hundred. A hectolitre is 100 litres.
70466.m: A hectolitre holds a hundred litres.

70467.q: How many centilitres are there in a litre?
70467.e: A litre has 10 decilitres and a decilitre has 10 centilitres. 10 · 10 = 100 cl.
70467.m: A hundred centilitres fit into one litre.

70468.q: How much liquid do 4 bottles of 7.5 dl each hold altogether?
70468.m: Large amounts in decilitres are converted into litres.

70486.q: What is the solution of the equation 7x − 4 = 3x + 20?
70486.e: You subtract 3x and add 4. This gives 4x = 24 and x = 6.
70486.m: You solve a linear equation by isolating the variable step by step.

70488.q: What is the solution of the equation x/4 − 3 = 2?
70488.e: You add 3 and get x/4 = 5. Multiplying by 4 gives x = 20.
70488.m: You get rid of a fraction in an equation by multiplying by the denominator.

70491.q: What is the solution of the equation 0.5x + 1.5 = 6?
70491.e: You subtract 1.5 and get 0.5x = 4.5. Dividing by 0.5 gives x = 9.
70491.m: Dividing by 0.5 is the same as doubling.

70570.q: What is the y-intercept of the line y = −3x + 7?
70570.e: The y-intercept is the value at x = 0: y = −3·0 + 7 = 7. The number −3 is the gradient.
70570.m: The y-intercept is the constant term of the equation of the line.

70573.q: A taxi charges a basic fare of 6 francs and 4 francs per kilometre. How much does a 12 km ride cost?
70573.e: The price is the linear function P(x) = 4x + 6. For x = 12, P = 48 + 6 = 54 francs.
70573.m: With fares that include a basic charge, the basic charge is the y-intercept.

70743.q: What does it mean when two shapes are congruent?
a: They are identical in shape and size.
They only have the same shape.
70743.e: Congruent shapes match in shape and size. You can lay one exactly on top of the other.

70769.q: When you roll a fair dice, what is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
70769.e: The favourable numbers are 5 and 6, so 2 of 6 equally likely outcomes. 2/6 simplified is 1/3.
70769.m: In a Laplace experiment you divide the number of favourable outcomes by the number of possible outcomes.

70774.q: A bag holds 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green balls. What is the probability of not drawing a blue ball?
70774.e: 3 + 2, so 5 of the 10 balls, are not blue. 5/10 is 1/2.
70774.m: Instead of counting the favourable cases, you can also look at the opposite event.

a: A group of jobs with similar tasks
A field where apprentices play sport
The list of all open apprenticeships
73031.e: An occupational field groups together jobs that have similar tasks, materials or workplaces. That makes it easier to find related jobs.
73031.m: An occupational field groups related jobs together.

73032.q: Which occupational field does the job of healthcare assistant (FaGe) belong to?
73032.e: Healthcare assistants care for and look after people in hospitals, care homes and home care services. That is why the job belongs to the health field.
73032.m: If you care for people, you work in the health field.

73033.q: Which job belongs to the construction field?
73033.e: Bricklayers build walls and buildings on the building site. That is why their job belongs to the construction field.
73033.m: Bricklayers work in the construction field.

73034.q: Which job fits the IT field?
73034.e: IT specialists develop programs or look after computers and networks. That is typical of the IT field.
73034.m: IT specialists program and look after computer systems.

73035.q: In which occupational field do farmers, gardeners and forest workers work?
73035.e: These jobs have to do with plants, animals, soil and forests. That is why they belong to the nature field.
73035.m: Jobs with plants, animals and forests belong to the nature field.

73036.q: Which job belongs to the hospitality field?
73036.e: Cooks prepare food in restaurants, hotels and canteens. That is part of hospitality.

73037.q: What do logistics workers EFZ mainly do?
73037.e: Logistics workers make sure goods arrive in the right place. They work in warehouses, at the post office or for transport companies.
73037.m: Logistics workers store and distribute goods.

73038.q: Why is it worth looking at a whole occupational field when choosing a career?
a: You discover related jobs you didn't know about
Because otherwise you won't get an apprenticeship
Because all jobs in the field pay the same
Because that is the only way into vocational school
73038.e: If you fix on just one job, you often overlook similar ones. The same field offers alternatives in case your dream job doesn't work out.
73038.m: Looking at the whole field shows you more options.

73039.q: Why is it important to know your own interests when choosing a career?
a: A job that interests you is more likely to be enjoyable
Because interests must be written in the apprenticeship contract
Because otherwise you may not write a CV
73039.e: If you are interested in the tasks of a job, you stay more motivated and learn more easily. That is why getting to know your own interests is a first step in choosing a career.
73039.m: Your interests show you which work you might enjoy.

73040.q: What is an example of a practical, hands-on strength?
a: Speaking well in front of people
73040.e: Hands-on strengths have to do with your hands and with tools. They are important, for example, in jobs such as joiner or mechanic.
73040.m: Practical skill shows in how you handle tools and materials.

73041.q: What is meant by social skills?
a: The ability to get on well with other people
73041.e: Social skills include teamwork, politeness and helpfulness, for example. They are important in almost every job.
73041.m: Social skills mean getting on well with other people.

73042.q: What is a good way to find out where your strengths lie?
a: Only look at how much a job pays
Take the same job as your best friend
Roll a dice and pick a job at random
73042.e: Parents, teachers or friends often see strengths you don't notice yourself. Your own view combined with other people's views gives a good picture.
73042.m: Feedback from others helps you recognise your strengths.

73043.q: Which quality is especially important for a job with lots of customer contact?
73043.e: Anyone who deals with lots of customers, for example in retail, should be friendly and open. That builds trust.
73043.m: With customers, friendliness is especially important.

73044.q: For which job is a head for heights especially important?
73044.e: Roofers work on roofs high up. If you are afraid of heights, you can put yourself and others in danger.
73044.m: If you work high up, you need a head for heights.

73045.q: What is meant by “self-assessment” when choosing a career?
a: You judge your own abilities yourself
A test marked by the training company
The mark from your class teacher
73045.e: In a self-assessment you think about what you are good at and like doing. It is often compared with how others assess you.
73045.m: In a self-assessment you judge yourself.

73046.e: Personal skills are about how you manage yourself, such as punctuality, reliability and determination. Training companies pay close attention to them.
73046.m: Reliability and staying power are important personal skills.

73047.q: What is an important aim of a taster apprenticeship?
a: To check whether the job really suits you
To take the final apprenticeship exam
73047.e: On a taster placement you see everyday working life up close. That way you notice whether the tasks and working environment match what you imagined.
73047.m: On a taster placement you check whether a job suits you.

73048.q: How do you usually get a taster apprenticeship?
a: You win one in a prize draw
You must start the apprenticeship first
73048.e: Young people usually organise taster placements themselves by phone, email or through online platforms. The careers advice service can help too.
73048.m: You usually arrange a taster placement yourself with the company.

73049.q: How should you behave on your first taster day?
a: Arrive on time and ask questions
Be as quiet as possible and ask nothing
Use your phone all the time
73049.e: Being on time and showing interest make a good impression. If you ask questions, you get to know the job better.
73049.m: On a taster placement, be on time and show interest.

73050.q: What do young people often get from the company after a taster apprenticeship?
a: An apprenticeship contract signed by the canton
73050.e: Many companies fill in an assessment form after the taster placement. You can later add good assessments to your application.
73050.m: Good taster reports strengthen your application.

73051.q: Why is it worth writing a taster diary or report after a taster placement?
a: You record what you liked and what you didn't
Because the apprenticeship contract requires it
Because otherwise you won't be paid
Because the report replaces the final mark
73051.e: A report helps you compare impressions and make better decisions later. It is also useful when talking to your parents and the careers adviser.
73051.m: A taster report helps you compare jobs.

73052.q: How long does a taster apprenticeship usually last?
a: A few days to about a week
73052.e: A taster placement usually lasts between one and five days. That is enough to get a good insight.
73052.m: A taster placement usually lasts only a few days.

73053.q: What makes sense if you didn't like a taster apprenticeship at all?
a: Think about what exactly didn't suit you
Give up choosing a career altogether
Never go on a taster placement again
Write the company a nasty message
73053.e: Even a bad experience is valuable, because you learn what you don't want. That way you can search more precisely.
73053.m: Even a disappointing taster placement helps you move on.

73054.q: Why is it good to try out several different jobs on taster placements?
a: You can compare the jobs with each other
Because that is the only way to get an ID card
Because every company pays for it
Because a single taster placement is not allowed
73054.e: If you get to know several jobs, you can compare them better and decide more confidently. You often discover new interests along the way.
73054.m: Several taster placements make it easier to compare jobs.

73055.q: What does the abbreviation BIZ stand for in career choice?
a: Bildungs- und Industriezentrale (education and industry office)
73055.e: At the careers information centre (BIZ) you find information about jobs, training and further education. It is run by the cantonal careers advice service.
73055.m: BIZ is short for careers information centre.

73056.q: Who runs the careers information centres in Switzerland?
73056.e: Careers, study and career-path advice is the cantons' responsibility. The careers information centres belong to these cantonal services.
73056.m: The BIZ belong to the cantonal careers advice service.

73057.q: What does a visit to the information library at the BIZ usually cost young people choosing a career?
73057.e: The information services of the careers information centres are free for young people choosing a career. That way everyone has access to careers information.
73057.m: The BIZ is free for young people choosing a career.

73058.q: What do you typically find at the BIZ?
73058.e: At the BIZ there is information material such as leaflets and films about many jobs. Experts also offer advice sessions.
73058.m: At the BIZ you find information and advice about jobs.

73059.q: Who works at the BIZ and advises young people?
73059.e: Trained careers, study and career-path advisers work at the BIZ. They support young people and adults with questions about training.
73059.m: At the BIZ, careers advice experts help you.

73060.q: What is the best way to prepare for an advice session at the BIZ?
a: Write down your own questions and interests
Bring an apprenticeship contract with you
73060.e: If you write down your questions and interests, you make better use of the session. School reports or taster reports are also helpful.
73060.m: Before the session, write down your questions and interests.

73061.q: Besides young people, who else may use the services of the BIZ?
a: Adults who want further training or a change of direction
73061.e: Careers, study and career-path advice is also there for adults. It helps with further training or changing jobs, for example.
73061.m: Adults can also get advice at the BIZ.

a: The official website of Swiss careers advice
A site only for university students
The website of a single company
73062.e: berufsberatung.ch is the official website of careers, study and career-path advice. There you find job descriptions, apprenticeships and tips for applying.
73062.m: berufsberatung.ch is the official website of Swiss careers advice.

73063.q: What is the apprenticeship listing on berufsberatung.ch called?
73063.e: LENA stands for “Lehrstellennachweis”, the apprenticeship listing. Training companies post open apprenticeships there, which you can search by job and place.
73063.m: You find open apprenticeships in the LENA listing.

73064.q: What do you find on berufsberatung.ch for each job?
a: A description with tasks and requirements
The phone number of every apprentice
The marks of all final exams
73064.e: For each job there is information on tasks, requirements, training and further education options. Photos and films often add to the description.
73064.m: On berufsberatung.ch you find a description of every job.

73065.q: In which national languages is berufsberatung.ch available?
73065.e: The website exists in German, French (orientation.ch) and Italian (orientamento.ch). That way it reaches young people in all the major language regions.
73065.m: berufsberatung.ch is also available in French and Italian.

73066.q: What can you find out with an interest test for choosing a career?
a: Which mark you will get in your report
Whether you will definitely get the apprenticeship
73066.e: In an interest test you answer questions about activities you enjoy. Afterwards you get suggestions for suitable jobs that you can look at more closely.
73066.m: An interest test shows you jobs that match your interests.

73067.q: What is the most important task of careers advice?
a: To support young people in choosing their training
To hand out apprenticeships to young people
73067.e: Careers advisers support young people so that they find suitable training. But the young people make the decision themselves.
73067.m: Careers advice supports you, but you decide yourself.

73068.q: What does “choosing a career is a process” mean?
a: It happens in several steps over a longer time
It is done in a single day
It is decided by a court
It only happens after the apprenticeship
73068.e: Choosing a career includes steps such as getting to know yourself, exploring jobs, taster placements, deciding and applying. It usually takes more than a year.
73068.m: Choosing a career happens in several steps.

73069.q: Where are open apprenticeships often advertised?
a: Only on posters at the station
73069.e: Open apprenticeships are mainly found on online job boards such as LENA, on company websites and through personal contacts.
73069.m: You find many apprenticeships on online job boards.

73070.q: When looking for an apprenticeship, what is a “speculative” or “blind” application?
a: An application without an advertised vacancy
73070.e: With a speculative application you apply to a company that has not advertised an apprenticeship. Sometimes this still leads to a chance.
73070.m: You can send a speculative application even without an advertised vacancy.

73071.q: Why is a network of relatives and acquaintances helpful when looking for an apprenticeship?
a: They often know about open apprenticeships
They may sign the apprenticeship contract
They can improve your school marks
73071.e: Many apprenticeships are filled through contacts before they are advertised publicly. That is why it is worth telling people around you what you are looking for.
73071.m: Tell the people around you which apprenticeship you are looking for.

73072.q: What does an application plan or application list show?
a: When and where you applied and how things stand
Your marks for the last three years
The holidays at the training company
73072.e: If you send lots of applications, it is easy to lose track. A list with the date, company and reply helps you follow up.
73072.m: An application list gives you an overview of your applications.

73073.q: Who signs the apprenticeship contract if the apprentice is not yet 18?
a: The parents or legal guardian as well
73073.e: For under-18s, the legal representative, usually the parents, must also sign the apprenticeship contract. After that the canton approves it.
73073.m: For under-18s, the parents also sign the apprenticeship contract.

73074.q: What should you do if you have accepted an apprenticeship and still have other applications open?
a: Tell the other companies and withdraw
Just let all the applications carry on
73074.e: Once you have accepted an apprenticeship, you politely withdraw your other applications. That way the companies can give the place to other young people.
73074.m: After accepting an offer, you withdraw your other applications.

73075.q: What should you do if a training company takes a long time to reply to your application?
a: Politely ask by phone or email
Just turn up at the company and start working
Send exactly the same application again
73075.e: After about two weeks with no reply, you may ask in a friendly way. That shows interest and commitment.
73075.m: Asking politely shows the company your interest.

a: The collection of all your application documents
A folder with all your apprenticeship contracts
The list of all training companies
73076.e: The application file includes the cover letter, CV, copies of reports and other evidence. It is the applicant's calling card.
73076.m: Your application file is your calling card for the training company.

73077.q: Besides the cover letter and CV, what else often goes into an application file?
73077.e: Besides school reports, many companies want to see taster assessments and aptitude test results. They show performance and effort.
73077.m: Taster reports and test results complete your file.

73078.q: In what form do many companies want applications today?
a: As a PDF by email or through an online portal
As a handwritten letter on wrapping paper
As a photo on social media
73078.e: Many training companies accept applications digitally. So you should have all your documents ready as neat PDFs.
73078.m: Keep your application documents ready as neat PDF files.

73079.q: Why should you include copies of your school reports in your file rather than the originals?
a: Companies are not allowed to read originals
73079.e: Application documents are not always sent back. That is why you include copies and keep the originals.
73079.m: Always include copies of your reports.

73080.q: What is especially important about an application file?
a: Complete, neat and free of mistakes
As colourful as possible with lots of smileys
As long as possible, at least 30 pages
73080.e: A tidy file with no mistakes shows care. Spelling mistakes, on the other hand, leave a bad impression.
73080.m: A neat file with no mistakes shows that you take care.

73081.q: Which email address is best for an application?
a: One with your first name and surname
73081.e: A serious email address with your own name looks professional. Nicknames can look unprofessional.
73081.m: For applications, use a serious email address with your name.

73082.q: What is a reference in an application file?
a: A person who can give information about you
An encyclopedia to look things up in
73082.e: References are, for example, teachers or taster companies who may give the company information about you. You ask their permission first.
73082.m: Always ask your referees for their permission first.

73083.q: Why should you adapt your application file a little for each company?
a: Because every company and job has different requirements
Because identical files are not allowed
Because otherwise you get no holidays
73083.e: A file tailored to the company shows real interest. The cover letter in particular should be individual.
73083.m: Adapt your application for each company.

73084.q: What goes into a CV for an apprenticeship?
a: Personal details, schooling, taster placements and hobbies
The wage you want for every year
The names of all your classmates
73084.e: A CV gives an overview of who you are and what you have done. For young people it includes schools, taster placements, languages, hobbies and references.
73084.m: Your CV shows your path so far at a glance.

73085.q: How long should a CV for an apprenticeship usually be?
73085.e: A CV should be short and clear. For school leavers, one page is usually enough, two at most.
73085.m: A good CV is short and clear.

73086.q: What do you call a CV set out as a table?
73086.e: Today the tabular CV is the norm. The details are set out clearly in columns and sections.
73086.m: Today a CV is usually written as a table.

73087.q: What should a photo on your CV show?
a: A holiday picture on the beach
A group photo with your class
73087.e: A serious, recent portrait photo looks friendly and professional. Selfies or party pictures are not suitable.
73087.m: Use a recent, serious portrait photo on your CV.

73088.q: Why is it worth mentioning hobbies on your CV?
a: Because otherwise the CV is invalid
73088.e: Hobbies say something about your personality. Team sports, for example, show you can work in a team, and an instrument shows staying power.
73088.m: Hobbies on your CV say something about your personality.

73089.q: Which detail belongs to the personal details on a CV?
73089.e: Personal details include name, address, phone number, email and date of birth. Nationality is often given too.
73089.m: Your date of birth belongs in the personal details.

73090.q: In what order are schools usually listed on a tabular CV?
a: Most recent school first, or in clear time order
73090.e: What matters is a clear order in time that is easy to follow. Often the most recent stage is listed at the top.
73090.m: Put the stages of your CV in clear time order.

73091.q: What is a sensible way to give your language skills on a CV?
a: With the language and your level
With the names of your language teachers
Not at all, languages don't matter
73091.e: For languages you state which language you know and how well, such as native language, good knowledge or basic knowledge. That helps the company assess you.
73091.m: For each language, say how well you know it.

73092.q: What is the aim of a cover letter?
a: To explain why you want this particular apprenticeship
73092.e: In the cover letter you give reasons why you are interested in the job and the company. It should make them want to meet you.
73092.m: In your cover letter you show why you want the place.

73093.q: How long should a cover letter be?
73093.e: A cover letter is short and to the point. One A4 page is usually enough.
73093.m: A cover letter is about one page long.

73094.q: Which greeting is best in a cover letter?
73094.e: If you know the name of the person responsible, address them directly, for example “Dear Ms Muster”. That comes across as personal and polite.
73094.m: In your cover letter, address the person responsible by name.

73095.q: What should you avoid as far as possible in a cover letter?
a: General phrases that would fit any company
A mention of your taster placement
73095.e: Phrases like “I am motivated and a team player” without an example say little. Concrete experiences, for example from your taster placement, are better.
73095.m: Concrete examples are more convincing than empty phrases.

73096.q: What belongs at the end of a cover letter?
a: A request for an interview and a closing
A list of all your school marks
A joke to lighten the mood
73096.e: At the end you say thank you and express the wish to have an interview. Then come the closing and your signature.
73096.m: End your cover letter by asking for an interview.

73097.q: Why should you write something about the company in your cover letter?
a: It shows that you have found out about it
Because the company doesn't know itself
73097.e: If you mention what appeals to you about the company, you show real interest. You can find information on its website or during a taster placement.
73097.m: Find out about the company before you write.

73098.q: Who should read a cover letter before you send it?
a: A second person to check it
The training company, before you write it
73098.e: A second person often finds mistakes you overlook yourself. Parents, teachers or careers advisers are happy to help.
73098.m: Have your cover letter checked by someone else.

73099.q: What is a suitable closing at the end of a cover letter?
73099.e: In formal letters in Switzerland people usually write “Freundliche Grüsse” (kind regards). Casual phrases are out of place.
73099.m: A formal letter ends with “Kind regards”.

73100.q: What is especially important at a job interview?
a: Arriving on time and well prepared
73100.e: Being on time and prepared shows respect and interest. Find out about the company and the job beforehand.
73100.m: Arrive at the interview on time and well prepared.

73101.q: Which question is asked very often in a job interview?
a: Why do you want to learn this job?
What car do your parents drive?
How much pocket money do you get?
73101.e: Training companies want to know why you have chosen the job. A convincing answer with examples is important.
73101.m: Prepare an answer to why you want to learn the job.

73102.q: What do you do if you don't understand a question in the interview?
73102.e: Asking is allowed and shows you want to be precise. A wrong answer to a misunderstood question looks worse.
73102.m: If you don't understand something, ask politely.

73103.q: Why is it good to ask questions yourself at the end of the interview?
a: It shows interest in the company
Because otherwise you lose the apprenticeship
Because it makes the interview longer
73103.e: Your own questions, for example about how the apprenticeship works or what the tasks are, show real interest. You should prepare a few questions.
73103.m: Prepare your own questions for the interview.

73104.q: What should you do with your phone during a job interview?
a: Switch it off or put it on silent and put it away
Put it on the table and read messages
Leave the sound on for important calls
73104.e: A ringing phone or using it looks rude. It should be switched off in your bag during the interview.
73104.m: Switch your phone off before the interview.

73105.q: What clothing is suitable for a job interview?
a: Clean clothes that suit the job
73105.e: Your clothes should be neat and suit the job. In a workshop they are different from in a bank, but always tidy.
73105.m: Dress neatly and to suit the job.

73106.q: How can you prepare well for a job interview?
a: Play video games late the night before
Not at all, it's all about being spontaneous
Don't look at the company beforehand
73106.e: A role play with parents, a teacher or friends takes away nerves. You practise typical questions and introducing yourself.
73106.m: Practise the interview beforehand in a role play.

73107.q: How do you greet the interviewer at the start?
a: With eye contact, a friendly greeting and your name
Not at all, you just sit down
73107.e: A friendly greeting with eye contact makes a good first impression. You introduce yourself by name.
73107.m: First impressions count, so greet people warmly with eye contact.

73108.q: What is an aptitude test for when looking for an apprenticeship?
a: It checks whether you meet the requirements of a job
It replaces the final apprenticeship exam
73108.e: Aptitude tests check school knowledge and abilities such as logic or spatial awareness. Many companies use the results to choose candidates.
73108.m: An aptitude test shows whether you meet a job's requirements.

73109.q: Which aptitude test is widely used by training companies in German-speaking Switzerland?
73109.e: The Multicheck is a well-known aptitude test for young people looking for apprenticeships in Switzerland. There are different versions for different types of job.
73109.m: The Multicheck is a well-known aptitude test for apprenticeships.

73110.q: What is often tested in aptitude tests?
73110.e: Typical parts are arithmetic, German, foreign languages, logic and concentration. Depending on the type of job, other tasks are added.
73110.m: Aptitude tests often test maths, language and logic.

73111.q: How can you prepare for an aptitude test?
a: Stay awake as long as possible the day before
Not at all, preparing is forbidden
73111.e: With sample tasks you get to know the type of questions. That gives you confidence and saves time in the test.
73111.m: Sample tasks help you with the aptitude test.

73112.q: What does a spatial awareness task test?
a: Whether you can turn shapes and objects in your head
73112.e: Spatial awareness is important in technical jobs, such as draughtsman or mechanic. You have to turn shapes and put them together in your mind.
73112.m: Spatial thinking is especially important in technical jobs.

73113.q: Who usually pays for an aptitude test such as the Multicheck?
a: Often the young people or their parents
73113.e: Many aptitude tests charge a fee, which is usually paid by the young people or their parents. Some cantons or companies offer support.

73114.q: What should you do if an aptitude test went badly?
a: Retake it later or score points with other strengths
Give up choosing a career at once
73114.e: A test only shows part of your abilities. You can often retake it and win people over with good taster reports.
73114.m: A weak test is no reason to give up.

73115.q: Which ability does a concentration task test?
a: Whether you can work accurately for a long time
73115.e: In concentration tasks you have to find certain symbols quickly and without mistakes, for example. That shows how carefully you work.

73116.q: How should you react to a rejection?
a: Stay calm and learn from it
73116.e: Rejections are normal when looking for an apprenticeship. The important thing is not to give up and to improve your application if necessary.
73116.m: Rejections are part of looking for an apprenticeship.

73117.q: What can you politely ask the company after a rejection?
73117.e: Many companies give brief feedback if you ask politely. That way you find out what you can do better next time.
73117.m: After a rejection, politely ask for the reason.

73118.q: What makes particular sense after several rejections?
a: Checking your application documents with a careers adviser
Hoping for just one single place
73118.e: Careers advisers can check applications and give new ideas. A related job might also be a good fit.
73118.m: After rejections, have your application checked.

73119.q: Why is a “plan B” sensible when choosing a career?
a: You have an alternative if your dream job doesn't work out
Because a plan A is not allowed
Because the canton requires two apprenticeships
Because you do two apprenticeships at once
73119.e: Things don't always work out with your dream job. If you have a related job or a bridging solution ready, you don't lose time.
73119.m: A plan B gives you security when looking for an apprenticeship.

73120.q: What is a good way to deal with frustration after a rejection?
a: Take your anger out on others
73120.e: Talking to parents, friends or teachers helps you deal with disappointment. After that, the next step is easier.
73120.m: Talk about disappointments, then the next step is easier.

73121.q: What does a rejection show in most cases?
a: That another applicant was a better fit
That you will never find an apprenticeship
73121.e: Often lots of young people apply for the same place, and the company has to choose. So a rejection is not a judgement on you as a whole person.
73121.m: A rejection is not a judgement on your worth.

73122.q: What is the best way to respond to a written rejection?
a: Say thank you briefly and politely
With a complaint to the newspaper
With a new application the same day
73122.e: A short thank you leaves a good impression. A place might come up later, and the company will remember you.
73122.m: Say thank you politely even after a rejection.

a: An interim solution between school and apprenticeship
A holiday camp run by the municipality
73123.e: Bridging programmes help young people who have no apprenticeship yet after compulsory school. They prepare them for training.
73123.m: A bridging programme leads from school to an apprenticeship.

73124.q: Which option is a well-known interim solution after compulsory school?
73124.e: In the 10th school year you can fill gaps in your schooling and carry on looking for an apprenticeship. It usually lasts one year.
73124.m: The 10th school year is a well-known interim solution.

a: A year of practice at a company with school days, before the apprenticeship
The first week of the apprenticeship
The exam before the apprenticeship contract
73125.e: In a pre-apprenticeship you usually work three to four days at a company and go to school for one to two days. It prepares you for an apprenticeship.
73125.m: A pre-apprenticeship combines work at a company with school.

a: A programme for young people without an apprenticeship, with practice and application training
73126.e: The motivation semester is for young people with no next step lined up. It combines work placements, lessons and support with looking for an apprenticeship.
73126.m: SEMO supports young people in looking for an apprenticeship.

73127.q: Which interim solution combines working for a family with learning a language?
a: A stay as an au pair
73127.e: As an au pair you live with a host family, help in the home and with the children, and learn a language at the same time. Many go to French-speaking Switzerland or abroad for this.
