a: As you like, for example with a course or by self-study
Only with three years of grammar school
Not at all, the exam needs no preparation
73357.e: For the central exam you can choose how to prepare. Many attend a preparation course, others study on their own. The exam covers general subjects such as languages, maths, sciences, history and geography.
73357.m: You can prepare for the central Passerelle however you like.

73358.q: Why is the supplementary exam after the vocational baccalaureate called the Passerelle?
a: The French word means bridge or crossing
It is the name of its inventor
It is a town in the canton of Vaud
73358.e: “Passerelle” is French for footbridge. The exam builds a bridge from the vocational baccalaureate to university.
73358.m: The Passerelle is a bridge to university.

73359.q: Which certificates entitle you to register for the Passerelle supplementary exam?
a: A vocational baccalaureate or a recognised specialised baccalaureate
An EFZ without a vocational baccalaureate
73359.e: People with a federal vocational baccalaureate certificate or a nationally recognised specialised baccalaureate certificate are admitted. An EFZ alone is not enough.
73359.m: For the Passerelle you need a vocational or specialised baccalaureate.

73360.q: With a vocational baccalaureate, what applies to access to higher education?
a: Universities of applied sciences are open, for university you need the Passerelle
All universities are open without any further exam
Only university is open, not universities of applied sciences
73360.e: The vocational baccalaureate opens the way to a university of applied sciences, usually in a matching field. For university and ETH you also need the Passerelle supplementary exam.
73360.m: Vocational baccalaureate: straight to a university of applied sciences, to university with the Passerelle.

73361.q: Which subject is examined in the Passerelle supplementary exam?
73361.e: The exam covers the first language, a second national language or English, mathematics, sciences, and the humanities and social sciences. Business subjects from the vocational baccalaureate are not examined again.
73361.m: The Passerelle mainly examines general Matura subjects.

73362.q: Which subjects belong to the humanities and social sciences area of the Passerelle?
73362.e: The humanities and social sciences area covers history and geography. Candidates already know subjects such as economics and law from the vocational baccalaureate.
73362.m: History and geography are part of the Passerelle exam.

73363.q: How long is the preparation course required for a Passerelle exam taken at a school?
73363.e: Anyone taking the exam at a recognised Matura school must attend the one-year preparation course there. For the central exam, preparation is up to you.
73363.m: The preparation course for the Passerelle usually lasts one year.

73364.q: Which qualification is a vocational baccalaureate together with a passed Passerelle legally equal to?
a: A bachelor's from a university of applied sciences
73364.e: Together with the vocational or specialised baccalaureate certificate, the Passerelle counts in Switzerland as equivalent to the grammar school Matura. Universities abroad decide for themselves whether to recognise it.
73364.m: With the Passerelle you are on a par with the grammar school Matura for university access.

73365.q: Which exam must you pass to receive a federal certificate (eidgenössischer Fachausweis)?
73365.e: The federal certificate is awarded after passing a federal professional exam (BP). It belongs to higher vocational education.
73365.m: If you pass the professional exam, you receive the federal certificate.

73366.q: Who runs the federal professional exams and draws up their exam regulations?
73366.e: Professional and industry associations, as professional organisations (OdA), develop and run the exams. That keeps the qualifications close to practice.
73366.m: Professional associations run the federal professional exams.

73367.q: Which authority approves the regulations of the professional exams?
73367.e: The exam regulations are approved by the State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation. This makes the qualifications federally recognised.
73367.m: The regulations of the professional exams need SERI's approval.

73368.q: What percentage of the eligible course costs for preparatory courses for a professional exam does the Confederation refund?
73368.e: Since 2018 the Confederation has supported candidates directly with half of the eligible course fees. The money goes to the person, not the school.
73368.m: The Confederation pays half the course costs for federal exams.

73369.q: To whom does the Confederation pay its contribution to preparatory courses for a professional exam?
a: Directly to the person who attended the course
To the school that offers the course
To the municipality where the person lives
73369.e: Since 2018 the support has gone directly to the candidates. The Confederation pays half of the eligible course costs, up to a maximum amount.
73369.m: The federal contribution for preparatory courses goes directly to the participants.

73370.q: Which condition must be met to receive the federal contribution to preparatory courses?
a: You must have taken the federal exam
You must have passed the exam with a 5
Your employer must apply for it
73370.e: The entitlement does not depend on passing, but the exam must be taken. You also need to be resident in Switzerland at the time of the exam and have the invoices in your own name.
73370.m: For the federal contribution, what counts is sitting the exam, not passing it.

73371.q: Which area of education does the federal certificate belong to?
73371.e: You get the federal certificate by passing a professional exam. This builds on an apprenticeship and work experience and therefore belongs to higher vocational education.
73371.m: The federal certificate is a qualification of higher vocational education.

73372.q: Besides an upper secondary qualification, what do most exam regulations require for admission to the professional exam?
a: Several years of work experience in the field
73372.e: The professional exam is aimed at professionals with practical experience. That is why the exam regulations usually require a few years of work experience after basic training.
73372.m: You are usually only admitted to the professional exam after a few years of work.

73373.q: Which exam leads to a federal diploma in higher vocational education?
73373.e: The advanced federal professional exam (HFP) is the most demanding federal exam in higher vocational education. Anyone who passes it receives a federal diploma.
73373.m: The advanced professional exam leads to the federal diploma.

73374.q: By which traditional name is the advanced federal professional exam known in many crafts?
73374.e: In crafts, the HFP often leads to titles such as federally certified master joiner. That is why it is called the master craftsman's exam.
73374.m: The master craftsman's exam in the crafts is an advanced professional exam.

73375.q: What share of the eligible course costs for an advanced federal professional exam does the Confederation cover?
73375.e: As with the professional exam, the Confederation refunds half of the eligible course fees. There is a maximum amount, and you must sit the exam.
73375.m: The Confederation pays half of the preparatory courses for federal exams.

73376.q: Which qualification in higher vocational education is more demanding?
73376.e: The advanced professional exam often builds on the professional exam and sets higher requirements. EBA and EFZ are qualifications of basic vocational training.
73376.m: The federal diploma is one level above the federal certificate.

73377.q: Which qualification do many advanced professional exams require for admission?
73377.e: The HFP often builds on the professional exam. Many exam regulations therefore require a federal certificate and additional work experience.
73377.m: The federal certificate is often the step before the federal diploma.

73378.q: Why may you not simply carry out electrical installations in buildings yourself?
a: Because mistakes can lead to fires or electric shocks
Because electricity is forbidden in Switzerland
Because cables may only be laid at night
Because only the municipality owns sockets
73378.e: Electrical installations require a permit and specialists with suitable training. Improper work can cause fires or life-threatening electric shocks.
73378.m: Electrical installations belong in the hands of specialists.

73379.q: Which title is gained with an advanced federal professional exam?
a: Certified tax expert with federal diploma
Finance and accounting specialist with federal certificate
73379.e: Tax expert with federal diploma is a qualification of the HFP. Federal certificates come from the professional exam, FH titles from universities of applied sciences.
73379.m: Federal diplomas can often be recognised by the label “eidg. dipl.” (federal diploma).

73380.q: Compared with the professional exam, what does an advanced professional exam typically qualify you for?
a: Running a business or expert roles
73380.e: The HFP sets higher requirements than the BP. It is aimed at specialists who want to run a business or work as an expert.
73380.m: The advanced professional exam prepares you for management and expert tasks.

73381.q: What was ETH Zurich called when it was founded?
73381.e: The school opened in 1855 as the Federal Polytechnic School. It has had its present name since 1911.
73381.m: ETH Zurich was originally called the Federal Polytechnic School.

73382.q: In which year did ETH Zurich start teaching?
73382.e: The law founding it was passed in 1854, and teaching began in October 1855. ETH was the first university of the young federal state.
73382.m: Teaching at ETH Zurich began in 1855.

73383.q: Which architect designed the main building of ETH Zurich?
73383.e: Gottfried Semper was a professor at the Polytechnic and built the main building between 1858 and 1864. Later Gustav Gull altered it considerably.
73383.m: The ETH main building is by Gottfried Semper.

73384.q: Which physicist gained his diploma at ETH Zurich in 1900?
73384.e: Albert Einstein studied at the Polytechnic from 1896 to 1900 and taught there as a professor from 1912 to 1914. He later received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
73384.m: Albert Einstein is the most famous graduate of ETH Zurich.

73385.q: Apart from the city centre, where is the second large site of ETH Zurich?
73385.e: The Hönggerberg is home to the departments of architecture, physics, chemistry and biology, among others. Since the start of the 21st century the campus has been expanded under the name Science City.
73385.m: ETH Zurich has its second campus on the Hönggerberg.

73386.q: Who runs ETH Zurich, unlike the cantonal universities?
73386.e: The two ETHs belong to the Confederation, which is why they are called “federal”. The ten universities, on the other hand, are run by the cantons.

73387.q: Roughly how many Nobel Prize winners are connected with ETH Zurich?
73387.e: According to ETH, 22 Nobel Prize winners are connected with the university because they studied, researched or taught there. This underlines its importance as a research university.
73387.m: Over 20 Nobel Prize winners have a link to ETH Zurich.

73388.q: In which city is the second Federal Institute of Technology besides ETH Zurich?
73388.e: The École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) is Switzerland's second federal institute of technology. Like ETH Zurich, it belongs to the Confederation.
73388.m: The second ETH is EPFL in Lausanne.

73389.q: Which research institute belongs to the ETH Domain?
73389.e: The ETH Domain includes ETH Zurich, EPFL and four research institutes: PSI, WSL, Empa and Eawag. CERN is an international organisation.
73389.m: The Paul Scherrer Institute is part of the ETH Domain.

73390.q: What is the science of teaching and learning for adults called?
73390.e: The term andragogy comes from the Greek word for man or human being. It separates adult learning from pedagogy for children.
73390.m: Andragogy is the study of adult learning.

73391.q: According to andragogy, what typically makes adult learning different from children's learning?
a: Adults learn in a self-directed way and build on their own experience
Adults can no longer learn anything new
Adults always need marks as a reward
73391.e: Adults bring a lot of life and work experience. They learn particularly well when the material is useful for their everyday lives and they can have a say.
73391.m: Adults learn best in a self-directed and practical way.

73392.q: What is meant by further education?
a: Learning after completing your first training
73392.e: Further education takes place after your first training, for example in courses, programmes or university further education. It helps you stay up to date in your job.
73392.m: Further education starts after your first training.

73393.q: According to the Further Education Act, who is mainly responsible for further education?
73393.e: The Further Education Act states that each person is first of all responsible for their own further education. Employers should support it, and the state helps in addition.
73393.m: You are first of all responsible for your own further education.

73394.q: According to the Further Education Act, which ability is one of the basic skills of adults?
73394.e: Basic skills include reading, writing and speaking in a national language, basic knowledge of mathematics and using digital media. The Confederation and the cantons support people in acquiring them.
73394.m: Arithmetic is one of the basic skills every adult needs.

73395.q: How many years of work experience does an adult without an apprenticeship need at least to be admitted to the EFZ qualification procedure?
73395.e: The Vocational Training Ordinance requires at least five years of work experience, part of it in the chosen trade. This allows adults to gain a vocational qualification later on.
73395.m: After five years of work experience, adults can gain an apprenticeship qualification later on.

73396.q: What is the procedure called in which adults prove their professional skills with a portfolio and so obtain a qualification?
73396.e: In validation, skills from work and everyday life are compared with the requirements of a trade. Missing parts can be made up with supplementary training.
73396.m: With validation of prior learning, work experience is recognised as a qualification.

73397.q: Which federal qualification qualifies you to lead courses in adult education?
a: Vocational trainer in a training company
73397.e: An adult educator with a federal certificate plans and leads learning sessions for adults. The qualification belongs to higher vocational education.
73397.m: If you want to teach adults, you can gain the federal certificate as an adult educator.

73398.q: What is an interest test used for in careers advice?
a: It shows which fields of work match your interests
It replaces the final apprenticeship exam
It decides which school you must go to
73398.e: An interest test asks what you like doing, for example working with people, technology or numbers. This points to fields of work you can look at more closely.
73398.m: Interest tests give ideas for suitable jobs.

73399.q: A person likes leading, persuading others and selling. Which career direction suits them particularly well?
73399.e: People who like leading and persuading have entrepreneurial interests. Suitable jobs exist in sales, marketing or running a business, for example.
73399.m: Interests give clues to suitable jobs.

73400.q: What does a career anchor describe?
a: A value that is particularly important to you at work
An exam at the end of an apprenticeship
73400.e: Career anchors are values such as security, independence or leadership. They help you make career decisions that suit you.
73400.m: Career anchors show what matters most to you at work.

73401.q: Why do people today talk about a career path rather than one job for life?
a: Because most people develop professionally several times during their lives
Because you may no longer work after an apprenticeship
Because every job disappears after five years
Because you have to change job every year
73401.e: Many people do further training, change job or profession and take on new roles. A career is therefore a lifelong development.
73401.m: A career develops over a whole lifetime.

73402.q: How can you best make use of unexpected opportunities for your career?
a: Stay curious and open and check out chances
Turn down every new possibility straight away
Only act according to a fixed plan
73402.e: Many career chances come up by chance, for example through a conversation or an internship. People who are curious, persistent and open are more likely to spot such opportunities.
73402.m: If you are open to chance, you discover new opportunities.

73403.q: What is the cantons' free service for a career check-up from the age of 40 called?
73403.e: viamia was introduced by the Confederation and the cantons and has been available throughout Switzerland since 2022. Career guidance experts assess your employability and give recommendations.
73403.m: With viamia, adults from 40 can review their career situation free of charge.

73404.q: What does the “M” stand for in the SMART goals method?
73404.e: SMART goals are specific, measurable, attractive, realistic and time-bound. Measurable goals are easier to check in career planning.
73404.m: A good career goal is measurable and has a deadline.

73405.q: What is a career step up called in which you mainly deepen expert knowledge instead of managing staff?
73405.e: Many companies offer a specialist career alongside the management career. There you move up as a specialist or expert without leading a team.
73405.m: Even without a management role, you can move up in a specialist career.

73406.q: From when do people not in work in Switzerland have to pay AHV contributions, for example during a gap year?
73406.e: Anyone not in work pays AHV contributions from 1 January after their 20th birthday. Missing years of contributions lead to a lower pension later.
73406.m: Even in a gap year, you need to think about AHV contributions from 21.

73407.q: How long does basic military training (recruit school) in the Swiss Army last for most recruits?
73407.e: Since the army's further development, recruit school usually lasts 18 weeks. Many do it between their apprenticeship or Matura and their studies.
73407.m: Recruit school lasts 18 weeks for most people.

73408.q: How much longer than military service does civilian service last in Switzerland?
73408.e: Civilian service lasts one and a half times the training service in the army not yet completed. The longer duration counts as proof of the conflict of conscience.
73408.m: Civilian service lasts one and a half times as long as military service.

73409.q: What is an au pair stay?
a: Helping in a host family in return for board, lodging and pocket money
A paid internship at a large company
A language course with hotel accommodation
An exchange semester at a university
73409.e: Au pairs live with a host family, look after children and help in the household. Alongside this they usually attend a language course.
73409.m: As an au pair you live with a host family and learn a language.

73410.q: What is a gap year in French-speaking Switzerland to learn French traditionally called in German-speaking Switzerland?
73410.e: In the past, many young people spent a year as a household helper or at a school in western Switzerland. Today there are programmes for this with language courses and internships.
73410.m: The Welschlandjahr is a classic gap year for learning French.

73411.q: Which official diploma certifies knowledge of French?
73411.e: The DELF (Diplôme d'études en langue française) is awarded by the French Ministry of Education. TOEFL is for English, DELE for Spanish and the Goethe-Zertifikat for German.
73411.m: If you learn French in a gap year, you can take the DELF.

73412.q: What is a year out after school called in the English-speaking world?
73412.e: A gap year is a year that fills a gap between two stages. It is often used for travel, internships, volunteering or language stays.
73412.m: A gap year is a deliberate break between two stages of education.

73413.q: What is a semester called in which students stay enrolled but do not attend any classes?
73413.e: You can apply for a leave semester for internships, military service or travel, for example. Your enrolment remains in place.
73413.m: With a leave semester you can briefly interrupt your studies without deregistering.

73414.q: Who pays out unemployment insurance daily allowances in Switzerland?
73414.e: The RAV is responsible for placement, advice and checks on jobseekers. The daily allowances are paid by an unemployment fund that you can choose freely.
73414.m: The RAV finds jobs, the unemployment fund pays out the money.

73415.q: What percentage of insured earnings is the unemployment insurance daily allowance for people who have to support children?
73415.e: Anyone who has to support children receives a daily allowance of 80 per cent of insured earnings. Without children the rate can fall to 70 per cent.
73415.m: With children, the unemployment insurance daily allowance is 80 per cent of insured earnings.

73416.q: How many months of contributions within two years do you usually need for unemployment benefit?
73416.e: Anyone who has paid contributions for at least 12 months within the two-year framework period meets the contribution requirement. Exceptions apply, for example, after education or illness.
73416.m: For unemployment benefit you usually have to have paid contributions for a year.

73417.q: Who pays jobseekers in Switzerland the unemployment insurance daily allowances?
73417.e: The RAV advises jobseekers and finds them jobs. The daily allowances, however, are paid by an unemployment fund that you can choose yourself.
73417.m: The RAV finds jobs, the unemployment fund pays the daily allowances.

73418.q: How many days is the general waiting period in unemployment insurance before the first daily allowance is paid?
73418.e: In principle there is a general waiting period of five days of registered unemployment. Depending on income and duty to support others, it can be shorter or longer.
73418.m: The general waiting period before the first daily allowance is basically five days.

73419.q: What must jobseekers prove to the RAV every month?
73419.e: Jobseekers must show that they are applying enough for a new job. Insufficient efforts can lead to days without benefit.
73419.m: If you are registered with the RAV, you must regularly prove your applications.

73420.q: From which unemployment rate in an occupation has the obligation to report vacancies applied since 2020?
73420.e: Employers must first report vacancies in such occupations to the RAV. The threshold was 8 per cent at the start in 2018 and was lowered to 5 per cent in 2020.
73420.m: If unemployment in an occupation is high, vacancies must be reported to the RAV.

73421.q: For how long do jobseekers registered with the RAV have a head start on information about vacancies that must be reported?
73421.e: Vacancies that must be reported may only be advertised publicly after five working days. During this time only jobseekers and the RAV can see the adverts.
73421.m: Jobseekers hear about reportable vacancies five working days earlier.

a: You keep learning after school and training
You stay at school until you die
You must take an exam every year
You only learn as a child and never again
73422.e: The world of work is constantly changing. If you keep learning in courses, at work or in everyday life, you stay up to date.
73422.m: Learning does not stop after your training.

73423.q: Which pillar is one of the four pillars of education in UNESCO's Delors Report of 1996?
73423.e: The Delors Report names learning to know, learning to do, learning to live together and learning to be. These pillars apply to all stages of life.
73423.m: According to UNESCO, education should also teach living together.

73424.q: Which psychologist described the forgetting curve?
73424.e: In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus showed with experiments that we quickly forget what we have learned. Regular revision slows down forgetting.
73424.m: Without revision, you quickly forget what you have learned.

73425.q: What does the abbreviation MOOC stand for?
73425.e: MOOCs are online courses that very many people can take at the same time, often free of charge. Swiss universities such as EPFL also offer such courses.
73425.m: A MOOC is an open online course for very many participants.

73426.q: What applies to the taxation of work-related further education costs you pay yourself in Switzerland?
a: You can deduct them up to a maximum amount
You must pay extra tax on them
The state always pays them in full
They have no effect on taxes
73426.e: Work-related further education costs that you pay yourself can be deducted from your income up to a maximum amount. This lowers your taxes.
73426.m: Further education costs lower your taxes.

73427.q: What is learning called that happens without a course, through experience in everyday life or at work?
73427.e: Formal learning leads to recognised qualifications, non-formal learning takes place in courses without such qualifications. Informal learning happens along the way, for example when solving problems at work.
73427.m: You are always learning in everyday life too; this is called informal learning.

73428.q: Which principle of responsibility comes first in the Further Education Act?
a: Further education is the responsibility of the individual
Further education is solely the state's business
Only trade unions organise further education
Further education is compulsory for all adults
73428.e: According to the Further Education Act, individuals are first of all responsible for their own further education. Employers should support them, and the state steps in to help in addition.
73428.m: In Switzerland, each person is first of all responsible for their own further education.

73429.q: Which learning method uses flashcards in compartments that are revised less and less often as your knowledge grows?
73429.e: Sebastian Leitner developed the learning card box with several compartments. Cards you know move to the next compartment and are revised less often, wrong ones start again from the beginning.
73429.m: With a learning card box, you revise exactly what you cannot do yet.

73430.q: Which law forms the basis for all other laws in Switzerland, including the Further Education Act?
73430.e: The Federal Constitution is at the top of the Swiss legal system. Since 2006 it has also contained an article on further education, on which the Further Education Act is based.
73430.m: All federal laws are based on the Federal Constitution.

73431.q: What is at the very bottom of the food pyramid, meaning you need the most of it?
73431.e: The bottom level is the widest. That is where unsweetened drinks such as water are, and we need the most of them.
73431.m: Water is at the very bottom of the pyramid.

73432.q: What is at the very top of the food pyramid, meaning you need the least of it?
73432.e: The top is the smallest level. You should only eat a little of sweets, crisps and sugary drinks.
73432.m: Sweet things are at the very top and are just for now and then.

73433.q: How many portions of vegetables and fruit should you eat a day?
73433.e: 5 portions a day are recommended, namely 3 portions of vegetables and 2 portions of fruit.
73433.m: Five portions of vegetables and fruit a day keep you healthy.

73434.q: Roughly how big is one portion of fruit?
73434.e: A portion is about as much as fits in your hand, for example an apple.
73434.m: A portion of fruit fits roughly in your hand.

73435.q: Which level of the food pyramid do bread, rice and pasta belong to?
73435.e: Bread, rice and pasta are made from grain. They give you energy for a long time.
73435.m: Bread, rice and pasta belong to grains.

73436.q: Which food is a dairy product?
73436.e: Yoghurt is made from milk. Cheese and quark are dairy products too.
73436.m: Yoghurt, cheese and quark are dairy products.

73437.q: Which food belongs to oils and fats in the pyramid?
73437.e: Butter is a fat. Oils and fats are near the top, so you only need a little of them.
73437.m: You only need a little oil and butter.

73438.q: How many portions of bread, rice, pasta or potatoes should you eat a day?
73438.e: 3 portions a day are recommended. Wholegrain foods keep you full for especially long.
73438.m: Three portions of grains or potatoes a day give you energy.

73439.q: What is the food pyramid for?
73439.e: The pyramid shows what you should eat a lot of and what you should eat only a little of. That way you eat a balanced diet.
73439.m: The food pyramid shows how to eat healthily.

73440.q: What is the small afternoon snack called in Switzerland?
73440.e: You eat the Zvieri in the afternoon, at about four o’clock. The word comes from Swiss German for ‘at four o’clock’.
73440.m: In the afternoon there is the Zvieri.

73441.q: Which fruit can you peel easily with your fingers for a morning snack?
73441.e: The peel of a mandarin comes off easily with your fingers. For pineapple, coconut and watermelon you need a knife or a tool.
73441.m: You can peel a mandarin without a knife.

73442.q: What is the best way to take your morning snack to school?
a: In a paper bag full of water
73442.e: In a box the food stays clean and does not get squashed. You can use the box again and again.
73442.m: A snack box keeps your snack clean.

73443.q: Which vegetable is good to nibble raw as a snack?
73443.e: You can eat carrots raw and they are good for nibbling. Potatoes are only eaten cooked.
73443.m: Raw carrots make a tasty snack.

73444.q: What is a mid-morning snack good for?
a: It gives you energy for learning
It gives you a stomach ache
73444.e: After breakfast, the body needs some energy again during the morning. With a snack you can learn better.
73444.m: A mid-morning snack gives you energy for the morning.

73445.q: What is breakfast called in Swiss German?
73445.e: Zmorge means something like ‘eating in the morning’. It is the first meal of the day.
73445.m: Breakfast is called Zmorge in Swiss German.

73446.q: In which season are strawberries harvested in Switzerland?
73446.e: Here, strawberries ripen from May and especially in June. None grow outdoors in winter.
73446.m: Swiss strawberries are available in early summer.

73447.q: In which season are most apples harvested in Switzerland?
73447.e: Apples ripen in late summer and autumn. After that they are stored so that they can be eaten for a long time.

73448.q: Which big orange vegetable is harvested in autumn and hollowed out at Halloween?
73448.e: Pumpkins are harvested in autumn. They are made into soup or carved.
73448.m: The pumpkin is a typical autumn vegetable.

73449.q: When are there fresh cherries from the tree in Switzerland?
73449.e: In Switzerland cherries ripen in June and July. Then you can pick them straight from the tree.

73450.q: What is roasted at street stalls in winter and eaten hot?
73450.e: Sweet chestnuts are roasted in autumn and winter and eaten warm.
73450.m: Hot roasted chestnuts are a winter treat.

73451.q: Which vegetable is harvested in Switzerland in spring?
73451.e: Asparagus grows from April to June. Pumpkins and Brussels sprouts are harvested in autumn and winter.

73452.q: Why is it good to buy fruit and vegetables that are in season?
a: They do not come from far away
They keep for a whole year
73452.e: Seasonal fruit and vegetables grow nearby. They do not have to be transported far and often taste better.
73452.m: Seasonal fruit and vegetables travel only a short way.

73453.q: Which fruit does not grow in Switzerland and comes from far away by ship?
73453.e: Bananas need a warm climate, so they do not grow here. Apples, pears and plums grow here.
73453.m: Bananas come to us from far away.

73454.q: In which season are plums ripe?
73454.e: Plums ripen in August and September. That is when there is plum tart.
73454.m: Plums are ripe in late summer.

73455.q: What is the best drink for quenching your thirst?
73455.e: Water has no sugar and quenches your thirst best. The body needs it every day.
73455.m: Water is the best thirst quencher.

73456.q: Can you drink tap water in Switzerland?
73456.e: Tap water in Switzerland is carefully checked. You can drink it without worrying.
73456.m: In Switzerland you can drink tap water.

73457.q: Where does most of Switzerland’s drinking water come from?
73457.e: About 80 per cent of drinking water comes from groundwater and springs. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
73457.m: Our drinking water mostly comes from the ground.

73458.q: When do you need to drink especially much?
73458.e: In hot weather and during sport you sweat. Your body loses water, which you need to replace.
73458.m: In hot weather and during sport you need to drink more.

73459.q: How can you tell that your body needs water?
73459.e: Thirst is a signal from the body. It tells us that we should drink.
73459.m: Thirst shows that your body needs water.

73460.q: Why is too much sugary drink not good?
a: It contains a lot of sugar
73460.e: Sugary drinks contain a lot of sugar. That harms your teeth and does not really fill you up.
73460.m: Sugary drinks contain a lot of sugar.

73461.q: Roughly how much water is in a human being?
73461.e: More than half of the body is made of water. That is why you have to drink every day.
73461.m: More than half of your body is made of water.

73462.q: What is best to take with you so you can drink water when you are out?
73462.e: You can refill a water bottle again and again. That also saves rubbish.
73462.m: You can refill a water bottle again and again.

73463.q: On which side of the plate do you put the fork?
73463.e: The fork goes to the left of the plate. The knife goes on the right.
73463.m: The fork goes to the left of the plate.

73464.q: On which side of the plate do you put the knife?
73464.e: The knife goes to the right of the plate, because most people hold it in their right hand.
73464.m: The knife goes to the right of the plate.

73465.q: Which way does the blade of the knife point when you lay the table?
a: Towards the edge of the table
73465.e: The blade points towards the plate. That way nobody cuts themselves.
73465.m: The knife blade points towards the plate.

73466.q: Where does the drinking glass go in a place setting?
a: Under the plate on the left
73466.e: The glass goes at the top right, above the knife. That way you can reach it easily with your right hand.
73466.m: The glass goes at the top right, above the knife.

73467.q: Where does the dessert spoon go in a place setting?
73467.e: The dessert cutlery lies across the top of the plate. You only need it at the end.
73467.m: The dessert spoon lies across the top of the plate.

73468.q: What do you put next to the plate for wiping your mouth?
73468.e: You use the napkin to wipe your mouth while eating. It goes next to or on the plate.
73468.m: You use the napkin to wipe your mouth.

73469.q: What do you need to eat soup?
73469.e: Soup is liquid. With a spoon you can scoop it up and eat it.
73469.m: You eat soup with a spoon.

73470.q: What do you do with the dirty dishes after a meal?
a: Put them dirty in the cupboard
73470.e: After eating, you clear the table. The dishes go into the sink or the dishwasher.
73470.m: After a meal you help clear the table.

73471.q: Where do vegetable peelings such as carrot peel go?
73471.e: Vegetable peelings are green waste. They are made into compost or biogas.
73471.m: Vegetable peelings go in the green waste.

73472.q: Where do you take an empty jam jar?
73472.e: Jars go to the glass recycling. New glass is made from them there.
73472.m: Empty jars go in the glass recycling.

73473.q: By which colours is glass sorted for recycling in Switzerland?
73473.e: The glass container has holes for clear, green and brown glass. That way it can be recycled better.
73473.m: Glass is sorted into clear, green and brown.

73474.e: Newspapers are made of paper. New paper is made from waste paper.
73474.m: Old newspapers go in the waste paper.

73475.q: What is the bag called for rubbish that cannot be recycled?
73475.e: Leftover rubbish goes in the rubbish bag. It is burned at the waste incineration plant.
73475.m: Whatever is not recycled goes in the rubbish bag.

73476.q: What is made from green waste and vegetable peelings?
73476.e: Compost is made from green waste. It is good soil for the garden.

a: So that it can be recycled
So that the bin gets heavier
73477.e: Sorted rubbish can be recycled. That way fewer new raw materials are needed.

73478.q: Which symbol is often found on things that can be recycled?
73478.e: The recycling symbol is made of three arrows going round in a circle. It shows that a material can be used again.
73478.m: Three arrows in a circle are the symbol for recycling.

73479.q: What is made from waste paper?
73479.e: Waste paper is soaked and made into new paper. That way fewer trees have to be felled.

73480.q: What should you do with a PET bottle before taking it away?
a: Squash it flat and put the lid on
73480.e: Squashed bottles take up less space. You screw the lid back on.
73480.m: Squash PET bottles flat before you take them away.

73481.q: Where do empty aluminium drink cans go?
73481.e: Aluminium can be melted down again and again. This takes much less energy than making new aluminium.
73481.m: Aluminium cans go in the aluminium collection.

73482.q: What do you do with a broken mobile phone?
a: Take it back to the shop
Throw it in the glass recycling
73482.e: Electrical devices contain valuable materials. Shops take old devices back.
73482.m: Old electrical devices are taken back to the shop.

73483.q: What is even better than recycling?
73483.e: Best of all is when no rubbish is made at all. For example, by using a water bottle instead of lots of single-use bottles.
73483.m: It is best to make little rubbish.

73484.q: Where do empty cardboard boxes go?
73484.e: Cardboard is collected and made into new cardboard. You fold the boxes flat.
73484.m: Empty cardboard boxes go in the cardboard collection.

73485.q: Why do you write a shopping list?
a: So that you don’t forget anything
So that you can buy more
So that the shop knows what you want
73485.e: Everything you need is on the list. That way you don’t forget anything and don’t buy things you don’t need.
73485.m: With a shopping list you won’t forget anything.

73486.q: What is best to do before you write your shopping list?
73486.e: In the fridge you can see what is still there and what is missing. That way you don’t buy things twice.
73486.m: Look in the fridge before you write your list.

73487.q: What is best to take with you when you go shopping?
73487.e: With your own bag you don’t need new bags. That saves rubbish.
73487.m: Take your own bag when you go shopping.

73488.q: A loaf of bread costs 3 francs and a milk costs 2 francs. How much do they cost together?
73488.m: When shopping, you add the prices together.

73489.q: You buy 3 apples at 50 centimes each. How much do you pay?
73489.e: 3 times 50 centimes is 150 centimes. That is 1 franc and 50 centimes.

73490.q: You pay for something costing 4 francs with a 5-franc coin. How much change do you get?
73490.m: Change is the difference between the money you pay and the price.

73491.q: Where do you find yoghurt and milk in the shop?
73491.e: Yoghurt and milk have to stay cool. That is why they are in the chiller cabinet.
73491.m: Dairy products are in the chiller cabinet.

73492.q: When should you wash your hands?
73492.e: You wash your hands before eating so that no germs get into the food.
73492.m: You wash your hands before eating.

73493.q: What do you need to wash your hands properly?
73493.e: Soap loosens dirt and germs from the skin. Water rinses them away.
73493.m: You wash your hands with water and soap.

73494.q: How long should you rub your hands with soap?
73494.e: For clean hands, rub them with soap for at least 20 seconds. That is about as long as singing ‘Happy Birthday’ twice.
73494.m: Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds.

73495.q: When must you always wash your hands?
73495.e: Germs get onto your hands on the toilet. That is why you always wash them afterwards.
73495.m: You always wash your hands after the toilet.

73496.q: Why do you wash your hands before cooking?
a: So that no germs get into the food
So that the food gets saltier
So that the cooker gets warm
73496.e: There are invisible germs on your hands. They should not get into the food.
73496.m: Clean hands keep germs away from food.

73497.q: Which places do people often forget when washing their hands?
73497.e: Thumbs, fingertips and the spaces between the fingers are often forgotten. You should rub them specially.
73497.m: Don’t forget your thumbs when washing.

73498.q: What do you do with your hands after washing them?
73498.e: After washing, you dry your hands well with a clean towel.
73498.m: After washing, dry your hands well.

73499.q: Roughly how cold should it be in the fridge?
73499.e: The fridge should be at most about 5 degrees Celsius. Then food stays fresh. Minus 18 degrees is the temperature in the freezer.
73499.m: The fridge is about 5 degrees cold.

73500.q: Where do vegetables and lettuce go in the fridge?
a: In the vegetable drawer at the bottom
In the door at the top
73500.e: The vegetable drawer is right at the bottom. Vegetables and lettuce stay nice and fresh there.
73500.m: Vegetables go in the vegetable drawer at the bottom.

73501.q: Where do you keep ice cream?
73501.e: Ice cream melts when it is warm. In the freezer, at about minus 18 degrees, it stays frozen.
73501.m: Ice cream is kept in the freezer.

73502.q: Why should you close the fridge door again quickly?
a: So that the cold stays inside
So that the light goes out
So that the food gets warm
73502.e: When the door is open, warm air flows in. The fridge then uses more electricity.
73502.m: Close the fridge door again quickly.

73503.q: Which food must go in the fridge?
73503.e: Opened milk goes off quickly in the warmth. Pasta, rice and sugar are stored dry in the cupboard.

73504.q: Which fruit is better not kept in the fridge?
73504.e: Bananas don’t like the cold and quickly turn brown in it. They are kept at room temperature.
73504.m: Bananas are not kept in the fridge.

73505.q: What do you do with food that has gone mouldy?
a: You give it to the dog
You put it in the vegetable drawer
73505.e: Mould can make you ill. You don’t eat mouldy food.

73506.q: What do you use to whip cream?
73506.e: With a whisk you stir quickly. That gets air into the cream and it becomes stiff.
73506.m: You whip cream with a whisk.

73507.q: What do you use to roll dough out flat?
73507.e: A rolling pin is a wooden roller. It makes the dough thin and flat.
73507.m: You roll out dough with a rolling pin.

73508.q: What do you use to peel potatoes and carrots?
73508.e: A peeler only cuts off a thin layer. That way lots of the vegetable is left.
73508.m: You peel vegetables with a peeler.

73509.q: What do you use to drain pasta?
73509.e: In a colander the hot water runs out through the holes. The pasta stays inside.
73509.m: You drain pasta in a colander.

73510.q: What do you use to grate cheese?
73510.e: A grater has sharp holes. When you rub the cheese over it, you get fine pieces.
73510.m: You grate cheese with a grater.

73511.q: Which way do you turn the handle of a pan on the cooker?
73511.e: A handle pointing outwards is easy to knock. Then the hot pan can fall down.
73511.m: Turn pan handles inwards on the cooker.

73512.q: What must not go in the microwave?
73512.e: Metal can make sparks in the microwave. That is dangerous.
73512.m: Metal does not belong in the microwave.

73513.q: What do you use to hold hot pans and baking trays?
73513.e: Oven gloves are thick and protect your hands from the heat. That way you don’t burn yourself.
73513.m: You hold hot things with oven gloves.

73514.e: Grains such as wheat are finely ground in a mill. That is how flour is made.
73514.m: Flour is made from ground grains.

73515.q: Where is grain ground into flour?
73515.e: At the mill, the grains are crushed between rollers or stones. The miller turns them into flour.
73515.m: At the mill grain becomes flour.

73516.q: Which machine harvests the grain in the field?
73516.e: The combine harvester cuts the grain and separates the grains from the straw.
73516.m: The combine harvester harvests the grain.

73517.e: Yeast is made of tiny fungi. They make gas bubbles, and the dough becomes big and airy.

73518.q: What is the classic Swiss plaited Sunday bread called?
73518.e: Zopf is plaited from strands of dough. Many families eat it for breakfast on Sundays.
73518.m: Zopf is a plaited Sunday bread.

73519.q: Who bakes bread as a job?
73519.e: The baker kneads the dough and bakes it in the oven. The miller makes the flour beforehand.

73520.q: What is the job called of someone who makes cheese?
73520.e: The cheesemaker makes cheese from milk in the cheese dairy. This takes a lot of knowledge and experience.

73521.q: What is the yellowish liquid called that is left over when making cheese?
73521.e: When the milk thickens, it separates into curds and whey. The whey is skimmed off.
73521.m: Whey is left over when making cheese.

73522.q: Where does Emmental cheese get its holes from?
73522.e: While the cheese ripens, bacteria in it make a gas. The gas bubbles form the holes.
73522.m: The holes in Emmental are made by gas.

73523.q: Where does a wheel of cheese ripen until it is ready?
73523.e: The wheels often lie in the cool cellar for months. They are looked after and turned.
73523.m: Cheese ripens in a cool cellar.

73524.q: What is the hut on the alp called where cheese is made in summer?
73524.e: In summer the cows are up on the alp. In the alpine hut the milk is made straight into alpine cheese.
73524.m: On the alp, alpine cheese is made in summer.

73525.q: Which three nutrients provide the body with energy?
73525.e: Carbohydrates, fats and protein contain energy the body can use. Vitamins, minerals and water provide no energy.
73525.m: Only carbohydrates, fats and protein provide energy.

73526.q: Which substance makes up about 60 per cent of an adult’s body weight?
73526.e: An adult’s body is about 50 to 60 per cent water. In children the share is even a little higher.
73526.m: Our body is mostly made of water.

73527.q: What are nutrients called that the body only needs in very small amounts, such as vitamins?
73527.e: The body needs vitamins and minerals only in milligrams or micrograms, so they are called micronutrients. Carbohydrates, fats and protein are macronutrients.
73527.m: The body needs micronutrients only in tiny amounts.

73528.q: Which nutrient mainly serves the body as building material for muscles and cells?
73528.e: Protein provides the building blocks for muscles, skin, hair and many other parts of the cells. That is why it is also called a building material.
73528.m: Protein is the body’s most important building material.

73529.q: What are the colour, scent and defence substances in fruit and vegetables called that are thought to be good for health?
73529.e: Plants make substances such as carotenoids or flavonoids to protect or colour themselves. These phytochemicals are also thought to be good for human health.
73529.m: Colourful fruit and vegetables contain valuable phytochemicals.

73530.q: Where on a food package do you find the information on energy, fat, sugar and protein?
73530.e: The nutrition table shows how much energy and how many nutrients are contained, usually per 100 grams or 100 millilitres. The list of ingredients, by contrast, says what the product is made of.
73530.m: The nutrition table tells you how many nutrients a food contains.

73531.q: In which order are the ingredients given on a list of ingredients?
73531.e: The ingredient with the largest share by weight comes first, the smallest last. That way you can tell, for example, whether sugar is the main ingredient.
73531.m: Whatever comes first on the list of ingredients is the biggest part.

73532.q: What is the main job of vitamins and minerals in the body?
73532.e: Vitamins and minerals control many processes in the body, such as the immune system or metabolism. That is why they are also called protective and regulating substances.
73532.m: Vitamins and minerals are protective and regulating substances.

73533.q: What is the sugar called that is carried in the blood and is also known as grape sugar?
73533.e: Glucose is a simple sugar and the most important sugar in the blood. It is also called grape sugar or dextrose.
73533.m: The scientific name for grape sugar is glucose.

73534.q: Which sugar is naturally found in milk?
73534.e: Milk sugar is called lactose. People with lactose intolerance find it hard to digest.

73535.q: What is the scientific name for ordinary household sugar from sugar beet?
73535.e: Household sugar is made of sucrose, a double sugar of glucose and fructose. In Switzerland it is mainly obtained from sugar beet.

73536.q: What is the carbohydrate called that is stored in large amounts in potatoes, rice and grains?
73536.e: Plants store energy in the form of starch, a complex sugar. Potatoes, rice, maize and grains are therefore important sources of starch.
73536.m: Potatoes and grains contain a lot of starch.

73537.q: In what form does the human body store carbohydrates in the liver and muscles?
73537.e: The body joins extra glucose together into glycogen and stores it in the liver and muscles. When needed, it is broken back down into glucose.
73537.m: Our body stores carbohydrates as glycogen.

73538.q: Where does the digestion of starch begin in the body?
73538.e: Saliva contains amylase, which splits starch into smaller sugar parts. That is why bread tastes slightly sweet after chewing it for a long time.
73538.m: Starch digestion already begins in the mouth when you chew.

73539.q: Why do wholegrain products keep you full longer than white flour products?
73539.e: Wholegrain contains the outer layers of the grain with lots of fibre. This makes blood sugar rise more slowly and you stay full for longer.
73539.m: Thanks to fibre, wholegrain keeps you full longer.

73540.q: What is the sugar called that is mainly found in fruit and honey?
73540.e: Fructose is also called fruit sugar. It is found in fruit and honey and tastes sweeter than household sugar.

73541.q: Which organ needs especially large amounts of glucose as a source of energy?
73541.e: The brain normally gets its energy almost only from glucose. It uses about a fifth of the energy the body needs at rest.
73541.m: The brain needs a lot of glucose for energy.

73542.q: What building blocks are proteins made of?
73542.e: Proteins are long chains of amino acids. During digestion the body breaks them down and builds its own proteins from them.
73542.m: Proteins are made of amino acids.

73543.q: What are amino acids called that the body cannot make itself?
73543.e: Essential amino acids have to be taken in with food. The body cannot make them itself.
73543.m: We have to eat essential amino acids.

73544.q: Which plant foods are especially rich in protein?
73544.e: Pulses such as lentils, beans, peas and chickpeas contain a lot of protein. They are an important source of protein in a plant-based diet.
73544.m: Pulses are good plant sources of protein.

73545.q: Why does the egg white turn white and firm when you fry an egg?
a: The protein sets because of the heat
73545.e: Heat changes the shape of the protein molecules and they set (denature). The clear egg white turns white and firm.

73546.q: Roughly how much protein do adults need per kilogram of body weight per day?
73546.e: Expert bodies recommend about 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day for adults. So a person weighing 60 kg needs about 48 grams.
73546.m: Adults need about 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day.

73547.q: Which combination especially improves the protein quality of a plant-based meal?
73547.e: Pulses and grains contain different amino acids and complement each other well. Examples are lentils with rice or beans with maize.
73547.m: Pulses and grains complement each other for protein.

73548.q: What are the proteins in the body called that speed up chemical reactions such as digestion?
73548.e: Enzymes are proteins that act as tools in the body to speed up reactions. Digestive enzymes, for example, break food down into small parts.
73548.m: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions in the body.

73549.q: Which grain protein makes bread dough stretchy and cannot be tolerated by people with coeliac disease?
73549.e: Gluten is a sticky protein in wheat, spelt, rye and barley. With coeliac disease, the gut cannot tolerate gluten.
73549.m: Gluten is the sticky protein in grain.

73550.q: Which vitamins can the body only absorb well together with fat?
73550.e: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble. That is why a little oil on a carrot salad makes sense.
73550.m: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

73551.q: Which fats are usually liquid at room temperature?
73551.e: Vegetable oils contain lots of unsaturated fatty acids, so they are liquid at room temperature. Animal fats such as butter have more saturated fatty acids and are solid.
73551.m: Oils with lots of unsaturated fatty acids are liquid.

73552.q: Of which oil do the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024) recommend at least one tablespoon a day, because it contains lots of omega-3 fatty acids?
73552.e: Rapeseed oil has a good ratio of omega-3 to omega-6 fatty acids. 2 tablespoons of vegetable oil a day are recommended, at least 1 tablespoon of which should be rapeseed oil.
73552.m: Rapeseed oil provides valuable omega-3 fatty acids.

73553.q: Which fish is a good source of omega-3 fatty acids?
73553.e: Oily sea fish such as salmon, herring and mackerel contain lots of omega-3 fatty acids. Lean freshwater fish such as perch, zander or pike contain much less.
73553.m: Oily sea fish such as salmon provides omega-3 fatty acids.

73554.q: In which foods is cholesterol found?
73554.e: Only humans and animals make cholesterol. It is found, for example, in egg yolk, butter and meat, but not in vegetable oils.
73554.m: Cholesterol is found only in animal foods.

73555.q: What is a fine mixture of fat and water, such as mayonnaise, called?
73555.e: In an emulsion, tiny droplets of fat and water are finely spread out. In mayonnaise, the lecithin from the egg yolk holds them together.
73555.m: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil and water.

73556.q: Why should fat be used only sparingly in the diet?
a: It has the highest energy density
73556.e: One gram of fat provides about twice as much energy as one gram of carbohydrate or protein. So too much fat quickly leads to an energy surplus.
73556.m: Fat provides the most energy per gram.

73557.q: What are harmful fats called that can form mainly when oils are partially hardened?
73557.e: Trans fatty acids form when vegetable oils are partially hardened and when they are heated strongly. They increase the risk of heart and circulation diseases, so their content is limited in Switzerland.
73557.m: Trans fats are unhealthy and should be avoided.

73558.q: Which disease did sailors used to get from a lack of vitamin C?
73558.e: On long sea voyages there was no fresh fruit or vegetables. The lack of vitamin C led to scurvy, with bleeding gums and poor wound healing.
73558.m: A lack of vitamin C causes scurvy.

73559.q: Which vitamin can the body make itself in the skin with the help of sunlight?
73559.e: UV light from the sun allows the skin to make vitamin D. It is important for strong bones.
73559.m: With sunlight, the skin makes vitamin D.

73560.q: Which vitamin is especially important for seeing in dim light?
73560.e: Vitamin A is needed for the visual pigment in the retina. A lack of it can lead to night blindness.
73560.m: Vitamin A is important for good eyes.

73561.q: Which vitamin is found almost only in animal foods, so that vegans should take a supplement?
73561.e: Vitamin B12 is made by bacteria and gets into our food mainly through meat, fish, eggs and dairy products. A supplement is recommended for a vegan diet.
73561.m: On a vegan diet, vitamin B12 must be supplemented.

73562.q: Which vitamin is needed for blood clotting?
73562.e: Vitamin K helps blood clot when you are injured, so that a wound closes. It is found mainly in green leafy vegetables.
73562.m: Vitamin K makes sure blood can clot.

73563.q: What does the body make vitamin A from, which is found in carrots, for example?
73563.e: Carrots contain a lot of beta-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A. The body turns it into vitamin A when needed.
73563.m: Beta-carotene is the precursor of vitamin A.

73564.q: Why shouldn’t you boil vegetables for too long in lots of water?
73564.e: Vitamin C and many B vitamins dissolve in the cooking water and are sensitive to heat. Cooking briefly in a little water protects them.

73565.q: Which of these foods contains especially much vitamin C per 100 grams?
73565.e: Red peppers contain more vitamin C than oranges, often over 100 milligrams per 100 grams. Cucumbers and bananas contain much less.
73565.m: Peppers are very rich in vitamin C.

73566.q: Which B vitamin is especially important for cell division and making blood, and is found in green leafy vegetables?
73566.e: Folic acid (vitamin B9) is needed for cell division and making blood. The name comes from the Latin word for leaf, because it is found in leafy vegetables.
73566.m: Folic acid is found mainly in green leafy vegetables.

73567.q: Which mineral is the most important building material for bones and teeth?
73567.e: Bones and teeth are largely made of calcium compounds. In Switzerland, dairy products are an important source of calcium.
73567.m: Calcium makes bones and teeth strong.

73568.q: Which mineral is part of the red blood pigment haemoglobin?
73568.e: Iron is built into haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood. People who lack iron are often tired and pale.
73568.m: Iron helps the blood carry oxygen.

73569.q: Which trace element does the thyroid gland need, and is added to table salt in Switzerland?
73569.e: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make hormones. Because Swiss soils contain little iodine, table salt has been iodised since 1922.
73569.m: Iodised salt supplies the thyroid with iodine.

73570.q: Which thyroid disease used to be very common in many Swiss mountain valleys?
73570.e: If the thyroid lacks a certain trace element, it swells up in the neck and a goitre develops. Since this trace element has been added to table salt, goitre has become rare in Switzerland.
73570.m: A goitre is an enlarged thyroid gland.

73571.q: Which substance is often also added to table salt in Switzerland to protect teeth from decay?
73571.e: Fluoride hardens tooth enamel and so protects against decay. That is why you can buy fluoridated table salt in Switzerland.

73572.q: According to the World Health Organization, what is the most salt you should eat per day?
73572.e: The WHO recommends no more than 5 grams of salt a day, which is about a teaspoon. In Switzerland many people eat a lot more.
73572.m: More than a teaspoon of salt a day is too much.

73573.q: Which mineral, together with chloride, is the main part of table salt?
73573.e: Chemically, table salt is sodium chloride. Too much sodium can raise blood pressure.
73573.m: Table salt is made of sodium and chloride.

73574.q: Which mineral is important for the muscles and is found in large amounts in nuts and wholegrain?
73574.e: Magnesium is needed for muscles and nerves to work. Nuts, wholegrain products and pulses contain a lot of it.
73574.m: Magnesium is important for muscles and nerves.

73575.e: Fibre is made up of parts of plants that our body cannot digest, or hardly at all. It is still important for healthy digestion.
73575.m: Fibre is the indigestible part of plants.

73576.q: Roughly how much fibre should adults eat per day?
73576.e: Expert bodies recommend at least about 30 grams of fibre a day for adults. Many people eat much less.
73576.m: Adults should eat about 30 grams of fibre a day.

73577.q: What should you drink if you eat lots of fibre?
73577.e: Fibre binds water and swells up in the gut. Without enough fluid, this can lead to constipation.
73577.m: If you eat lots of fibre, you must drink enough.

73578.q: Which of these foods contains no fibre at all?
73578.e: Fibre is only found in plant foods. That is why cheese, meat, eggs and butter contain no fibre.

73579.q: What is the soluble fibre in apples called, which is also used to set jam?
73579.e: Pectin is found in apples, quinces and citrus fruits. It binds water and makes jam set.

73580.q: What in the gut partly feeds on fibre?
73580.e: Much fibre is broken down in the large intestine by useful bacteria. It is food for healthy gut flora.
73580.m: Fibre is food for the gut bacteria.

73581.q: What is the insoluble fibre called that plant cell walls are mainly made of?
73581.e: Cellulose is the main part of plant cell walls. Humans cannot digest it, but it keeps the gut active.
73581.m: Plant cell walls are mainly made of cellulose.

73582.q: Why do growing children and teenagers need more energy per kilogram of body weight than adults?
a: The body needs energy to grow
73582.e: While growing, the body builds new bones, muscles and other tissues. For this it needs extra energy and enough nutrients.

73583.q: What does the energy density of a food tell you?
a: How much energy is in a certain amount
73583.e: Energy density says how many kilocalories or kilojoules a food provides per gram or per 100 grams. Vegetables have a low energy density, nuts and chocolate a high one.
73583.m: Energy density shows how much energy is in one gram of food.

73584.q: What is the energy called that the body needs at complete rest for breathing, heartbeat and body warmth?
73584.e: The basal metabolic rate is the energy needed at rest. When you move, the body needs extra energy.
73584.m: The basal metabolic rate is the energy needed at complete rest.

73585.q: A muesli contains 50 g carbohydrates, 10 g fat and 10 g protein. 1 g fat provides 9 kcal, and 1 g carbohydrate or protein 4 kcal each. How many kilocalories is that?
73585.e: 50 times 4 makes 200 kcal, 10 times 9 makes 90 kcal and 10 times 4 makes 40 kcal. Together that is 330 kcal.
73585.m: You work out the energy by multiplying each nutrient by its energy value.

73586.q: In which unit is energy measured in the International System of Units?
73586.e: The official unit of energy is the joule, named after James Prescott Joule. On food it usually appears as kilojoules (kJ) next to the kilocalories.

73587.q: Roughly how many kilojoules are equal to one kilocalorie?
73587.e: One kilocalorie is exactly 4.184 kilojoules, so about 4.2 kJ. 100 kcal is therefore about 420 kJ.

73588.q: What happens in the long run if you regularly eat more energy than you use?
a: Your weight definitely stays the same
73588.e: The body stores extra energy mainly as fat. The energy balance is then positive.
73588.m: If you eat more energy than you need, you gain weight.

73589.q: Which activity increases the energy you need the most?
73589.e: Exercise clearly increases the energy you use. When reading, watching TV or sleeping, you use only a little more than your basal metabolic rate.
73589.m: Exercise increases the energy you need.

73590.q: How much unsweetened drink does the Swiss food pyramid recommend for adults per day?
73590.e: About 1 to 2 litres of unsweetened drinks a day are recommended, ideally tap water or tea. In hot weather and during sport you need more.
73590.m: Drink 1 to 2 litres of unsweetened drinks a day.

73591.q: How many portions of vegetables and fruit does the Swiss food pyramid recommend per day?
73591.e: 5 portions a day are recommended, 3 of them vegetables and 2 fruit. One portion is about a handful.
73591.m: Eat 5 portions of vegetables and fruit every day.

73592.q: According to the Swiss dietary guidelines, roughly how much does one portion of vegetables or fruit weigh?
73592.e: One portion of vegetables or fruit is about 120 grams. That is about a handful.
73592.m: One portion of vegetables or fruit is about a handful.

73593.q: How many portions of dairy products do the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024) recommend per day?
73593.e: 2 to 3 portions of milk or dairy products a day are recommended, ideally unsweetened. One portion is, for example, 2 dl of milk or 30 g of hard cheese.
73593.m: 2 to 3 portions of dairy products a day are part of it.

73594.q: According to the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024), how often a week should you eat meat at most?
73594.e: Meat, including poultry and sausages, should be limited to 2 to 3 times a week. For protein you should vary between meat, fish, eggs, tofu and pulses.
73594.m: You should only eat meat 2 to 3 times a week.

73595.q: What is at the top of the Swiss food pyramid?
a: Sweet and salty snacks and sugary drinks
73595.e: Sweets, sugary drinks and salty snacks are right at the top. They are not necessary and should only be eaten in small amounts.
73595.m: Sweet and salty snacks belong at the top of the pyramid and only rarely on your plate.

73596.q: How many portions of grain products or potatoes do the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024) recommend per day?
73596.e: 3 portions of grain products or potatoes a day are recommended. At least half of the grain products should be wholegrain.
73596.m: Eat 3 portions of grains or potatoes a day, half of them wholegrain.

73597.q: According to the Swiss dietary guidelines (as of 2024), how often at least should you eat pulses?
a: At least five times a day
73597.e: Pulses such as lentils, beans and chickpeas should be eaten at least once a week. They provide protein and lots of fibre.
73597.m: Pulses belong on your plate at least once a week.

73598.q: In which season are Swiss outdoor-grown strawberries in season?
73598.e: Swiss outdoor strawberries are available from about May to July. In winter, strawberries are usually imported.
73598.m: Swiss strawberries are available in early summer.

73599.q: What does it mean to shop seasonally?
a: Buying produce that is ripe in the region right now
73599.e: Seasonal produce has grown in the region at the right time of year and been harvested ripe. It has short transport routes and usually needs no heated greenhouses.
73599.m: Shopping seasonally means buying what is ripe in the region right now.

73600.q: Which vegetable is a typical autumn vegetable in Switzerland?
73600.e: Pumpkins are harvested in late summer and autumn. After that they can be stored for a long time.
73600.m: Pumpkin is a typical autumn vegetable.

73601.q: Why do imported fruits transported by plane have a poor environmental record?
a: Air transport causes a lot of CO2
73601.e: Planes use a huge amount of fuel and emit a lot of CO2. Air-freighted goods harm the climate much more than goods that come by ship or lorry.
73601.m: Air-freighted goods harm the climate a lot.

73602.q: Why can tomatoes from a heated greenhouse in winter be worse for the climate than outdoor tomatoes in summer?
a: Heating uses a lot of energy
They are harvested in the dark
73602.e: Greenhouses have to be heated in winter, often with fossil fuels. Seasonal outdoor vegetables do not need this energy.

73603.q: Which aid shows when which fruit and vegetables are in season in Switzerland?
73603.e: A seasonal calendar lists, month by month, which fruit and vegetables are available fresh from the region. It helps with seasonal shopping.
73603.m: A seasonal calendar shows what is in season.

73604.q: Which vegetables are often harvested in Switzerland in autumn and sold as stored vegetables in winter?
73604.e: Carrots, cabbage, celeriac and beetroot can be stored for months after harvest. That way there are Swiss vegetables in winter too.
73604.m: Stored vegetables such as carrots are available from Switzerland in winter too.

73605.q: Which wild herb that smells of garlic is gathered in Swiss woods in spring?
73605.e: Wild garlic grows in damp deciduous woods in spring. You must carefully tell it apart from the poisonous lily of the valley and autumn crocus.
73605.m: Wild garlic is a spring herb from the woods.

73606.q: What is the highest temperature a fridge should have?
73606.e: At no more than about 5 °C, most bacteria multiply only very slowly. A fridge thermometer helps you check.
73606.m: The fridge should be no warmer than 5 degrees.

73607.q: What temperature should a freezer reach at least?
73607.e: Frozen food is stored at -18 °C or colder. At this temperature microorganisms cannot multiply.
73607.m: Frozen food is stored at -18 degrees or colder.

73608.q: Which bacteria are often found in raw eggs and raw poultry?
73608.e: Salmonella can cause stomach and gut illnesses. Cooking food thoroughly and good kitchen hygiene protect against them.
73608.m: Raw poultry and raw eggs can contain salmonella.

73609.q: Why should you use different chopping boards for raw meat and for salad?
a: Because otherwise the meat gets dry
73609.e: Otherwise germs from the raw meat can get onto food that will not be heated any more. This is called cross-contamination.
73609.m: Raw meat and salad belong on separate boards.

73610.q: What does ‘use by’ mean on a package?
a: After that date you shouldn’t eat it
It is usually still good for a long time afterwards
It is only ripe after that date
73610.e: The use-by date is found on perishable foods such as mince. You should not eat them after this date.
73610.m: After the use-by date, food no longer belongs on your plate.

73611.q: What does ‘best before’ mean on a package?
a: Until then the maker guarantees the quality
After that it is immediately poisonous
Only after that may you eat it
It must be cooked by then
73611.e: The best-before date is the maker’s guarantee of quality. Many foods are still fine to eat after it.
73611.m: After the best-before date, food is often still good.

73612.q: What should you do with a loaf of bread that has mould in one spot?
a: Toast the bread and eat it
73612.e: The threads of the mould grow invisibly through the whole airy loaf. Many moulds make toxins, so the whole loaf should be thrown away.
73612.m: Mouldy bread is thrown away completely.

73613.q: What is the process called in which milk is briefly heated to kill germs that cause disease?
73613.e: In pasteurisation, milk is briefly heated to about 72 to 75 °C. The process is named after Louis Pasteur.
73613.m: Pasteurisation makes milk safer by heating it briefly.

73614.q: What is cooking over hot steam called, without the food lying in the water?
73614.e: When steaming, the vegetables lie in a basket above boiling water. That way fewer vitamins and minerals are lost.

73615.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
73615.e: At sea level, water boils at 100 °C. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils at a little less than 100 °C there.
73615.m: At sea level water boils at 100 degrees.

73616.q: Which cooking method starts with searing and then continues covered with a little liquid, for example for a ragout?
73616.e: When braising, meat is first seared well and then cooked until tender, covered, in a little liquid. This creates roasted flavours and a sauce.
73616.m: When braising, you sear first and then cook in liquid.

73617.q: What is it called when you dip vegetables briefly in boiling water and then cool them in ice water?
73617.e: When blanching, vegetables are dipped only briefly in rapidly boiling water and then plunged into cold water. This keeps them crunchy and colourful, for example before freezing.
73617.m: Blanching means boiling briefly and cooling straight away.

73618.q: What is cooking in hot fat called, for example for chips?
73618.e: When deep-frying, the food floats in hot fat at about 160 to 180 °C. This makes it crispy on the outside.
73618.m: Chips are deep-fried in hot fat.

73619.q: What is cooking in hot but not boiling liquid called, for example for eggs without their shells?
73619.e: When poaching, delicate foods are cooked in liquid at about 65 to 75 °C. The water should not bubble.
73619.m: When poaching, you cook in hot, not boiling, liquid.

73620.q: What forms when you sear meat hard in a hot pan?
a: A brown crust with roasted flavours
73620.e: At high heat, sugars and protein building blocks react with each other. This creates the brown crust and the typical roast flavour.
73620.m: Searing creates browning and roasted flavours.

73621.q: Why does food cook faster in a pressure cooker than in an ordinary pan?
a: The pressure raises the boiling temperature
73621.e: In the closed pressure cooker the pressure rises. As a result, the water only boils at about 115 to 120 °C, and the food cooks faster.
73621.m: In a pressure cooker food cooks faster thanks to the higher pressure.

73622.q: What is cooking in its own juice or with a little liquid and some fat in a covered pan called?
73622.e: When stewing, vegetables cook at about 100 °C, covered, in a little liquid or their own juice. This protects flavour and nutrients.
73622.m: Stewing is cooking with a little liquid in a covered pan.

73623.q: What is the Bio Suisse label called?
73623.e: Bio Suisse awards the ‘Bud’ label (Knospe). In Switzerland it is the best-known sign for organic food.
73623.m: The Bud is the organic label of Bio Suisse.

73624.q: What is forbidden on a farm with the Bud label?
73624.e: Bud farms may not use synthetic chemical pesticides or artificial fertiliser. Manure, grazing and crop rotation, on the other hand, are part of organic farming.
73624.m: Organic farmers do without synthetic chemical sprays.

73625.q: Which kind of transport is generally not allowed for Bud products?
73625.e: Bio Suisse generally bans air transport because it causes a great deal of CO2. Imported Bud products therefore usually come by ship, rail or lorry.
73625.m: Bud products are generally not flown in.

73626.q: What rule does Bio Suisse have for a farm that wants to produce organically?
a: The whole farm must be organic
Only the animals must be organic
Only the farm shop must be organic
73626.e: Bio Suisse follows the whole-farm principle. A farm cannot be only partly organic but must convert completely.
73626.m: With the Bud, the whole farm converts to organic.

73627.q: What is the most important aim of the Fairtrade label?
a: Fair conditions for farmers in the South
The lowest possible prices in shops
73627.e: Fairtrade wants small farmers and workers in countries of the Global South to be paid more fairly and to have better working conditions. This includes minimum prices and a premium for community projects.
73627.m: Fairtrade stands up for fair wages and prices in the Global South.

73628.q: Under which name did Fairtrade start in Switzerland?
73628.e: The Max Havelaar Foundation was founded in Switzerland in 1992 and awards the Fairtrade label. The name comes from the main character of a Dutch novel.
73628.m: In Switzerland Max Havelaar stands for Fairtrade.

73629.q: What do farmers’ organisations receive with Fairtrade in addition to the sale price?
a: A discount on seed from Europe
73629.e: As well as the minimum price, Fairtrade pays a premium. The farmers decide together whether to use it to pay for schools, wells or better machines, for example.
73629.m: The Fairtrade premium goes into community projects.

73630.q: Which fruit is an especially successful Fairtrade product in Switzerland?
73630.e: Bananas grow in tropical countries and are one of the best-selling Fairtrade products in Switzerland. Apples, cherries and plums also grow in Switzerland.
73630.m: Fairtrade bananas are very common in Switzerland.

73631.q: What does the MSC label on fish products stand for?
73631.e: MSC stands for Marine Stewardship Council. The label is given to fish from wild stocks that are not overfished.
73631.m: The MSC label stands for sustainably caught wild fish.

73632.q: Which label recognises responsible fish farming, meaning fish from aquaculture?
73632.e: The ASC label (Aquaculture Stewardship Council) is meant for farmed fish. MSC is for wild-caught fish, FSC for wood and IP-Suisse for Swiss farm products.
73632.m: ASC stands for farmed fish and MSC for wild-caught fish.

73633.q: Which environmental organisation founded the MSC in 1997 together with a food company?
73633.e: The MSC was founded in 1997 by the WWF and the company Unilever. Since 1999 it has been an independent organisation.
73633.m: The WWF helped found the MSC.

73634.q: Which label is found on wood and paper from responsible forestry?
73634.e: FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) is given to wood and paper from forests that are managed sustainably.
73634.m: The FSC label stands for sustainably used forests.

73635.q: Which animal is shown in the IP-Suisse logo?
73635.e: IP-Suisse is an association of farmers who produce in a nature-friendly and animal-friendly way. Its symbol is a ladybird.
73635.m: The ladybird is the symbol of IP-Suisse.

73636.q: What does the ecological footprint measure?
a: The area you need for your lifestyle
The number of trees in a country
73636.e: The ecological footprint works out how much biologically productive area is needed to provide food, energy and goods and to absorb waste such as CO2.
73636.m: The footprint shows how much nature we need for our lives.

73637.q: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, roughly how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived as people do in Switzerland?
73637.e: According to the FOEN, almost three Earths would be needed if everyone consumed like the Swiss population. So Switzerland uses much more than nature can replace.
73637.m: The Swiss lifestyle needs almost three Earths.

73638.q: In which unit is the ecological footprint usually given?
73638.e: The footprint is given in global hectares. One global hectare is an area with the world’s average biological productivity.
73638.m: The footprint is measured in global hectares.

73639.q: The Swiss Mathis Wackernagel helped invent a well-known measure of how much nature we use. What is it called?
73639.e: Mathis Wackernagel developed the ecological footprint in the 1990s together with William Rees. It shows how much nature a person needs for their lifestyle.
73639.m: Mathis Wackernagel is one of the inventors of the ecological footprint.

73640.q: What does Earth Overshoot Day mean?
a: From this day nature’s yearly budget is used up
On this day the Earth is at its hottest
On this day there is the most rubbish
On this day nobody may drive a car
73640.e: On Earth Overshoot Day humanity has used as many resources as the Earth can renew in the whole year. For the rest of the year it lives at the expense of the future.
73640.m: After Earth Overshoot Day we are living on credit from nature.

73641.q: Which decision is most likely to make your ecological footprint smaller?
a: Travelling by train instead of by plane
73641.e: A flight causes much more greenhouse gas per person than the same distance by train. So choosing the train uses far fewer resources.
73641.m: Taking the train instead of flying protects the environment.

73642.q: What does a country’s biocapacity show?
