74363.q: What is the research field called that aims to make the decisions of AI systems understandable to people?
74363.e: Many learning systems are regarded as a ‘black box’ because the way they reach a decision is unclear. Explainable AI (XAI) is meant to make transparency and control possible.
74363.m: Explainable AI makes the reasons for a machine’s decision visible.

74364.q: Which writer formulated the three laws of robotics in 1942?
74364.e: The laws appeared in the short story ‘Runaround’. The first forbids a robot to injure a human; they are still quoted in AI debates today.
74364.m: Asimov’s laws of robotics are an early attempt to give machines a morality.

74365.q: Which organisation adopted the first legally binding international treaty on AI and human rights in 2024?
74365.e: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law is also open to states outside Europe. Switzerland helped to draft it.
74365.m: In 2024 the Council of Europe created the first binding international treaty on AI.

74366.q: What are deceptively real-looking fakes of videos, images or voices created with AI called?
74366.e: The term is made up of ‘deep learning’ and ‘fake’. Deepfakes are ethically problematic, for example, in disinformation, fraud or damaging someone’s reputation.
74366.m: Deepfakes are AI fakes that look real.

74367.q: What is the challenge called of designing AI systems so that their goals match human values?
74367.e: The alignment problem asks how to make sure that an AI does what people really want. Even small errors in setting the goal can lead to unwanted behaviour.
74367.m: Alignment is about tying AI to human values.

74368.q: Since when has the revised Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection been in force?
74368.e: The fully revised Data Protection Act brought Swiss law into line with digital developments and European standards. It now protects only data of natural persons.
74368.m: The new Swiss Data Protection Act has applied since September 2023.

74369.q: Which authority in Switzerland supervises compliance with data protection by federal bodies and private parties?
74369.e: The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC) can open investigations and, since 2023, issue binding orders. The cantons have their own data protection officers for cantonal bodies.
74369.m: The FDPIC watches over data protection in Switzerland.

74370.q: Since which date has the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applied?
74370.e: The GDPR was adopted in 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018. It also applies to Swiss companies that offer goods or services to people in the EU.
74370.m: The GDPR has applied since May 2018.

74371.q: What does the right to informational self-determination mean?
a: Each person basically decides for themselves about the disclosure and use of their data
The state decides what information you may read
Each person may freely use all data of others
Companies may sell data without consent
74371.e: The right was formulated in 1983 by the German Federal Constitutional Court in its census ruling. It also shapes Swiss and European data protection law.
74371.m: Informational self-determination means: I decide about my data.

74372.q: What is the principle called of processing only as much personal data as is needed for the purpose?
74372.e: Data minimisation is one of the basic principles of the GDPR and in Swiss law is part of proportionality. What is not collected cannot be misused.
74372.m: You should only collect the data you really need.

74373.q: What is the principle called of building data protection into a system technically right from its development?
74373.e: The concept was coined by the Canadian privacy commissioner Ann Cavoukian. The revised Swiss Data Protection Act explicitly requires data protection by design and privacy-friendly default settings.
74373.m: Data protection should be built into technology from the start.

74374.q: Which company used data from millions of Facebook profiles without consent for political advertising, as became known in 2018?
74374.e: Data from up to 87 million profiles were harvested through a quiz app. The scandal sparked worldwide debates about data power and election manipulation.
74374.m: The Cambridge Analytica scandal showed the political power of personal data.

74375.q: Which right did the European Court of Justice recognise in 2014 in the ‘Google Spain’ case?
74375.e: Under certain circumstances, search engines must remove links to outdated or inappropriate information about a person. This is weighed against the public interest in information.
74375.m: The right to be forgotten protects against old information being findable for ever.

74376.q: In which year did the Federal Council set up the National Advisory Commission on Biomedical Ethics (NEK)?
74376.e: The Federal Council set up the NEK on 3 July 2001. It advises politicians and the public on ethical questions in medicine and health care.

74377.q: Which area is the National Ethics Commission NEK responsible for in Switzerland?
74377.e: Its full German name means ‘National Ethics Commission in the Field of Human Medicine’, abbreviated CNE in French. It deals, for example, with questions at the end of life, vaccinations or organ donation.
74377.m: The NEK deals with ethical questions in human medicine.

74378.q: At which federal office is the NEK’s secretariat based?
74378.e: Administratively, the NEK is attached to the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) in Bern. In terms of content, it works independently and is not bound by instructions.
74378.m: The NEK is based at the FOPH but works independently.

74379.q: Who in Switzerland carries out the ethical review of individual research projects on humans, which the NEK explicitly does not do?
74379.e: Under the Human Research Act, cantonal ethics committees approve specific research projects. The NEK, by contrast, comments on fundamental questions and not on individual applications.
74379.m: Cantonal ethics committees review specific research projects.

74380.q: Which system for organ donation did the NEK recommend in 2019 instead of the opt-out system?
74380.e: In the declaration system, people are regularly asked to state their views on organ donation. The NEK considered the opt-out system ethically problematic because silence should not count as consent.
74380.m: In 2019 the NEK wanted people to state their views on organ donation explicitly.

74381.q: Which commission has dealt with ethical questions of biotechnology and genetic engineering in animals, plants and other organisms in Switzerland since 1998?
74381.e: The Federal Ethics Committee on Non-Human Biotechnology (ECNH) was set up by the Federal Council in 1998. It has dealt, for example, with the dignity of plants.
74381.m: The ECNH is responsible for biotechnology outside humans.

74382.q: What kind of body is the NEK?
74382.e: Extra-parliamentary commissions are expert bodies of the Confederation whose members are elected by the Federal Council. They contribute expertise without passing laws themselves.
74382.m: The NEK is an extra-parliamentary commission elected by the Federal Council.

74383.q: Which task is part of the NEK’s legal mandate?
74383.e: The NEK writes opinions, advises authorities on request and informs the public. In this way society should be able to discuss ethical questions in medicine widely.
74383.m: The NEK advises and promotes public debate on ethics.

74384.q: Which UN report of 1987 defined sustainable development as taking into account the needs of future generations?
a: Report to the Club of Rome
74384.e: The report ‘Our Common Future’, led by the Norwegian Gro Harlem Brundtland, gave the best-known definition: meeting the needs of the present without taking away the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
74384.m: Sustainable means leaving future generations their chances.

74385.q: What is the unspoken agreement called that the younger generation finances the pensions of the older one?
74385.e: The generational contract is not a real contract but an image for solidarity between age groups. It assumes that today’s contributors will also be provided for later.
74385.m: The generational contract links young and old in pension provision.

74386.q: Which instrument, accepted by the people in 2001, is meant to stop the Confederation permanently passing debts on to future generations?
74386.e: The debt brake was accepted with about 85 per cent yes and has been applied since 2003. Over an economic cycle, spending should not exceed revenue.
74386.m: The debt brake keeps federal finances in balance over time.

74387.q: Which association won a ruling of the European Court of Human Rights against Switzerland on 9 April 2024 for insufficient climate protection?
a: KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz (Senior Women for Climate Protection)
74387.e: The ECtHR found that Switzerland had violated the right to respect for private and family life because it was doing too little against climate change. The ruling is often discussed in connection with duties towards those affected and coming generations.
74387.m: The KlimaSeniorinnen won against Switzerland in Strasbourg in 2024.

74388.q: What is the procedure called of giving future costs and benefits less weight in calculations than present ones?
74388.e: The higher the discount rate, the less future climate damage counts today. That is why choosing the rate is an ethical question of justice between generations.
74388.m: Discounting makes future damage smaller in today’s calculations.

74389.q: Which popular initiative did Swiss voters accept on 3 March 2024?
a: Initiative for a 13th AHV pension payment
74389.e: The initiative was accepted with about 58 per cent, while the pensions initiative to raise the retirement age was clearly rejected on the same day. The debate focused strongly on sharing the burden between young and old.
74389.m: In 2024 the voters decided on a 13th AHV pension payment.

74390.q: Which country created the office of a commissioner for future generations by law in 2015?
74390.e: The ‘Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act’ requires public bodies to consider the long-term consequences of their decisions. A commissioner monitors this.
74390.m: Wales has its own commissioner for future generations.

74391.q: Which former employee of an NSA contractor made the worldwide mass surveillance by US intelligence services public in 2013?
74391.e: Edward Snowden handed journalists secret documents about programmes such as PRISM. He fled via Hong Kong to Russia and has lived there ever since.
74391.m: Snowden revealed the NSA’s mass surveillance in 2013.

74392.q: Which military analyst gave the ‘Pentagon Papers’ on the Vietnam War to the press in 1971?
74392.e: The secret study showed that several US governments had misled the public about the war. The Supreme Court allowed the press to publish it.
74392.m: In 1971 Ellsberg made the deception about the Vietnam War public.

74393.q: Which security guard in Zurich in January 1997 saved bank files from being shredded that were connected with dormant assets from the Nazi era?
74393.e: Christoph Meili worked as a night watchman at the Union Bank of Switzerland. After threats he was granted asylum in the USA, but later returned to Switzerland.
74393.m: In 1997 Christoph Meili became Switzerland’s best-known whistleblower.

74394.q: Which computer specialist took customer data from the HSBC private bank in Geneva and handed it to tax authorities?
74394.e: The data were later analysed internationally as ‘Swiss Leaks’. In 2015 the Federal Criminal Court convicted Falciani in his absence of economic espionage.
74394.m: Hervé Falciani’s data led to the Swiss Leaks.

74395.q: When did the EU adopt a directive to protect people who report breaches of EU law?
74395.e: The Whistleblower Directive requires secure reporting channels and forbids retaliation such as dismissal. Member states had to implement it by the end of 2021.
74395.m: Since 2019 the EU has protected whistleblowers with its own directive.

74396.q: What happened in 2020 in the National Council to the bill to protect whistleblowers in the private sector?
a: It went to a popular vote
It was handed over to the cantons
74396.e: The National Council sank the revision of the Code of Obligations after more than ten years of debate. For critics it did not go far enough, for others it went too far.
74396.m: In 2020 special protection for whistleblowers in the private sector failed in the National Council.

74397.q: To which body can employees of the federal administration report wrongdoing?
74397.e: Since 2011 the Federal Personnel Act has provided for a reporting office at the Swiss Federal Audit Office (SFAO). Anyone who reports in good faith must not be put at a disadvantage because of it.
74397.m: Federal employees can report wrongdoing to the Federal Audit Office.

74398.q: Under which code name did FBI deputy director Mark Felt help journalists uncover the Watergate affair?
74398.e: Mark Felt only revealed himself in 2005 as the source of Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein. The affair led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974.
74398.m: Deep Throat was the secret source in the Watergate scandal.

74399.q: What characterises a genuine moral dilemma?
74399.e: In a dilemma, you can fulfil only one of two well-founded duties and so inevitably violate the other. There is no way out without moral loss.
74399.m: In a dilemma, every choice violates a duty.

74400.q: Which psychologist used the Heinz dilemma to study the stages of moral development?
74400.e: In the Heinz dilemma, a man considers whether to steal an unaffordable medicine for his dying wife. Kohlberg was mainly interested in the reasoning behind the answer, not in the answer itself.
74400.m: Kohlberg assessed the reasoning in the Heinz dilemma.

74401.q: What is the highest level of moral development according to Lawrence Kohlberg called?
74401.e: At this level, people are guided by universal principles such as justice, even against existing rules. Kohlberg assumed that only a few adults reach it.
74401.m: Postconventional morality follows general principles rather than mere rules.

74402.q: What is the ancient thought experiment called in which two shipwrecked people fight over a plank that can carry only one?
74402.e: The Greek philosopher Carneades asked whether you may push the other person away to save yourself. In law, this is an example of an excusing necessity.
74402.m: The plank of Carneades asks whether you may save yourself at another’s expense.

74403.q: What is the problem described in the journal ‘Science’ in 1968 called, that freely accessible common goods are overused?
74403.e: When each person takes their own advantage from a shared pasture, it is destroyed for everyone. The economist Elinor Ostrom later showed that communities such as Swiss alpine pasture cooperatives can prevent this.
74403.m: Without rules, common goods risk being overused.

74404.q: What is the situation called in which two people questioned separately both end up worse off through selfish action than if they had cooperated?
74404.e: For each person individually, betrayal pays, but together keeping silent would be better. This model from game theory shows why trust and rules are important for cooperation.
74404.m: In the prisoner’s dilemma, self-interest leads both to a worse result.

74406.q: Which principle, going back to Thomas Aquinas, allows a good action under certain conditions despite a foreseeable bad side effect?
74406.e: The bad consequence must not be intended and must not be the means to the end, and there must be an appropriate reason. The principle is often applied in medical ethics and the ethics of war.
74406.m: Under the principle of double effect, what counts is what you intend and what you merely accept.

74407.q: What did the ecologist Garrett Hardin argue with his ‘lifeboat ethics’?
a: Aid from rich countries to poor ones should be limited
All people should share goods equally
Rich countries should take in unlimited refugees
Aid should only go through the churches
74407.e: Hardin compared rich countries to a lifeboat that sinks when overcrowded, and therefore rejected unlimited aid. His position was strongly criticised for its harshness.
74407.m: Lifeboat ethics asks whether aid may have limits.

74408.q: Which part of the computer do you use to type letters?
74408.e: On the keyboard there is a key for every letter. When you press it, the letter appears on the screen.
74408.m: You write letters and numbers with the keyboard.

74409.q: Where do you see the computer's pictures and texts?
74409.e: The screen shows everything the computer does. It is also called a monitor.
74409.m: The screen shows pictures and texts.

74410.q: What do you use to move the pointer on the screen?
74410.e: When you slide the mouse back and forth on the table, the pointer moves with it. With a click you choose something.
74410.m: You move the pointer with the mouse.

74411.q: Which device puts a text from the computer onto paper?
74411.e: The printer prints texts and pictures onto paper. That way you can hold them in your hand.
74411.m: The printer puts texts onto paper.

74412.q: Which part plays sounds and music?
74412.e: Sounds, voices and music come out of the loudspeaker. You can also plug in headphones.
74412.m: Sounds come out of the loudspeaker.

74413.q: Which part lets the computer record your voice?
74413.e: The microphone records sounds, for example your voice. That way you can talk to others or record a song.
74413.m: The microphone records sounds and voices.

74414.q: What is the part called that calculates and thinks inside the computer?
74414.e: The processor is a small chip in the computer. It carries out all the commands and calculates very fast.
74414.m: The processor is the computer's brain.

74415.q: What does a computer need to work at all?
74415.e: A computer only works with electricity. It gets it from the socket or from a battery.

74416.q: What is a computer called that you can fold shut and take with you?
74416.e: In a laptop, the screen, keyboard and battery are in one device. You can fold it shut and take it anywhere.
74416.m: You can fold a laptop shut and take it with you.

74417.q: Which set of instructions from everyday life is similar to an algorithm?
74417.e: A recipe says exactly which steps you have to do one after the other. An algorithm works in exactly the same way.
74417.m: A recipe is like an algorithm.

74418.q: What must the steps in an algorithm be like?
74418.e: A computer does not understand vague instructions. That is why every step must be clear and unambiguous.
74418.m: Every step in an algorithm must be clear.

74419.q: What do building instructions for blocks tell you?
74419.e: Building instructions show step by step which piece goes where. That is why they are like an algorithm.
74419.m: Building instructions show step by step how to build something.

74420.q: What happens if a step is missing from a set of instructions?
74420.e: If a step is missing, you do not know what to do. The result is then often wrong.
74420.m: Good instructions have no missing steps.

74421.q: What is the first step when brushing your teeth?
74421.e: First the toothpaste goes on the toothbrush. Only then can you brush your teeth.
74421.m: Brushing your teeth also has a fixed order.

74422.q: What does a computer do with an algorithm?
74422.e: The computer works through the steps of the algorithm exactly in order. It only does what is written there.
74422.m: A computer carries out algorithms step by step.

74423.q: An algorithm says: “Take 2 steps, then 3 more steps.” How many steps is that?
74423.e: You work out 2 + 3 = 5. So you take 5 steps in total.
74423.m: You can add up the steps of a set of instructions.

74424.q: What is a command for a computer?
74424.e: A command tells the computer what to do. Many commands one after the other make a program.
74424.m: A command tells the computer what to do.

74425.q: What do you call many commands for a computer one after the other?
74425.e: A program is made of many commands in a fixed order. The computer works through them one after the other.
74425.m: A program is made of many commands.

74426.q: What is the right order when getting dressed?
74426.e: The socks have to go on your feet first. Only then do the shoes fit over them.
74426.m: The order of commands is important.

74427.q: What happens if you swap commands around?
74427.e: The computer does exactly what is in the order given. If commands are swapped, something different often comes out.
74427.m: Swapped commands can lead to a wrong result.

74428.q: What do you call a mistake in a program?
74428.e: A bug is really a small insect. That is what people call a mistake in a program.
74428.m: A mistake in a program is called a bug.

74429.q: What do you call looking for mistakes in a program and fixing them?
74429.e: When debugging, you look for the bugs, meaning the mistakes, and correct them. After that the program works properly.
74429.m: When debugging, you find and fix mistakes.

74430.q: What is a loop in a program?
74430.e: In a loop, a command is repeated several times. That way you do not have to write it again each time.
74430.m: A loop repeats commands several times.

74431.q: A command “Clap!” is repeated 3 times. How many times do you clap?
74431.e: The command is carried out 3 times. That is why you clap 3 times.
74431.m: A repetition carries out the same command several times.

74432.q: What is the name of a well-known programming language with colourful blocks for children?
74432.e: In Scratch you put colourful command blocks together like jigsaw pieces. You can use it to program games and stories.
74432.m: In Scratch you program with colourful blocks.

74433.q: What does an educational robot do?
74433.e: You give an educational robot commands. It carries them out exactly as you entered them.
74433.m: An educational robot carries out the commands you give it.

74434.q: An educational robot is facing forwards. What does it do with the command “forwards”?
74434.e: With “forwards”, the robot moves one step in the direction it is facing.
74434.m: With the command forwards, the robot moves forwards.

74435.q: A robot is facing north and makes a quarter turn to the right. Which way is it facing now?
74435.e: If you turn a quarter turn to the right from north, you face east. To the left it would be west.
74435.m: To the right of north is east.

74436.q: A robot makes a quarter turn to the left twice. Which way is it facing then?
74436.e: Two quarter turns make a half turn. The robot then faces exactly the other way.
74436.m: Two quarter turns make a half turn.

74437.q: A robot moves 3 squares forwards and then 1 square backwards. How many squares is it from the start?
74437.e: It moves 3 forwards and 1 back. 3 minus 1 makes 2 squares.
74437.m: Moving backwards brings the robot closer to the start again.

74438.q: How does a small educational robot like Blue-Bot get its commands?
74438.e: With the Blue-Bot, you press arrow buttons on its back or use a tablet. Then you press Go.
74438.m: You give an educational robot commands with buttons.

74439.q: How far does the Blue-Bot move with one step forwards?
74439.e: The Blue-Bot and the Bee-Bot move about 15 centimetres per step. That is why there are matching play mats with squares.
74439.m: The Blue-Bot moves about 15 centimetres per step.

74440.q: Where does an educational robot get its energy from?
74440.e: Educational robots have a rechargeable battery or normal batteries. You charge the rechargeable battery with electricity again.
74440.m: An educational robot needs a rechargeable battery or batteries.

74441.m: In this sequence you always add 2.

74442.q: How does the pattern continue: circle, circle, star, circle, circle, ...?
74442.e: The pattern is always two circles, then one star. After two circles comes the star.
74442.m: In a pattern, a group repeats again and again.

74443.q: Secret code: A=1, B=2, C=3. Which word is 2 1?
74443.e: 2 stands for B and 1 stands for A. Together that makes BA.
74443.m: In a code, one sign stands for another.

74444.q: Which two digits does a computer calculate with inside?
74444.e: Inside, the computer only knows two states, on and off. They are written as 1 and 0.
74444.m: Inside, a computer calculates with 0 and 1.

74445.e: A QR code is a square made of black and white dots. A mobile phone can read it and, for example, open a website.
74445.m: A QR code is a picture code a mobile phone can read.

74446.q: Where do you find a barcode in a shop?
74446.e: There is a barcode on almost every packet. The till reads it and so knows the price.
74446.m: The till reads the barcode on the packaging.

74447.q: In Morse code there are dots and ...?
74447.e: Morse code is made up of short and long signals. They are written as dots and dashes.
74447.m: Morse code is made up of dots and dashes.

74448.q: How many answers are there to a yes-no question?
74448.e: You answer a yes-no question only with yes or no. Those are two possibilities.
74448.m: A yes-no question has two possible answers.

74449.q: Which question is a yes-no question?
74449.e: To “Do you have a dog?” you can only say yes or no. The other questions need a longer answer.
74449.m: You can answer a yes-no question with yes or no.

74450.e: An apple is a fruit. It grows on a tree and is not an animal.
74450.m: An apple is a fruit and not an animal.

74451.q: What do you call a plan that leads to a solution with yes-no questions?
74451.e: In a decision tree, you go one way for yes and the other way for no. In the end you reach the solution.
74451.m: A decision tree leads to the solution with yes-no questions.

74452.q: You are looking for a number from 1 to 4. After how many clever yes-no questions do you know it for sure?
74452.e: First ask: “Is it bigger than 2?” Then only 2 numbers are left, and a second question is enough.
74452.m: With clever questions you find the solution faster.

74453.q: What is a good first question for guessing an animal?
74453.e: The question “Can it fly?” divides many animals into two groups. That way lots of animals are ruled out at once.
74453.m: A good question divides the possibilities into two groups.

74454.q: If it rains, you take an umbrella. It is raining. What do you do?
74454.e: The answer to “Is it raining?” is yes. So the rule applies, and you take the umbrella with you.
74454.m: With yes you follow the rule, with no you do not.

74455.q: A small light has two states. Which ones?
74455.e: A small light is either on or off. That is like yes or no for a computer.
74455.m: On and off is like yes and no.

74456.q: Which numbers are sorted by size?
74456.e: In 1, 3, 5, 7 each number gets bigger. The smallest number is at the front.
74456.m: When sorting, the smallest number comes first.

74457.q: Which word comes first in alphabetical order?
74457.e: Apple begins with A. A is right at the front of the alphabet.
74457.m: In the alphabet, A is right at the front.
